speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Eudes Dube (Minister of Public Works):
subsubtopic: PICKERING TOWNSHIP SITE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO PROCEED WITH EXPROPRIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement regarding expropriation proceedings to acquire a site for a new Toronto airport at Pickering, Ontario. Hon. members will recall that public hearings of objections were held during December in Toronto, as provided for in the Expropriation Act, and the hearing officer's report was tabled in the House on January 18. The government has given careful and detailed consideration to the objections documented in the report, and in particular the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has reviewed the technical aspects. These issues, as well as the vitally important social implications, have been extensively reviewed by cabinet.
My colleague the Minister of Transport is today tabling two documents most pertinent to this issue: first, a technical response to the objections made at the public hearing, which was prepared by the Ministry of Transport; second, a statement by the Minister of Transport regarding the need for a new Toronto airport. This in turn clearly establishes the need for the land being expropriated.
The government is convinced of the need for a new Toronto airport and I am of the opinion the Pickering site is required for this purpose. Accordingly, I have signed the notices of confirmation of expropriation and requested the Attorney General of Canada to take the necessary steps immediately to effect registration of the notices in the local land registry and title offices.

These Notices include the majority of lands described in the notices of intention. However, certain portions of the lands described in the notices of intention are not being confirmed. The lands that are not therefore being expropriated are generally located on the original boundary and I am advised by the Minister of Transport it is not essential they be acquired for the airport. This advice is based upon investigations completed since the first announcement in March 1972. I might add that the owners of these lands will be offered the option of selling their land to the government.
In accordance with the procedures laid down in the Expropriation Act, written offers of compensation, accompanied by an appraisal report, will be made to every owner of an interest in the lands to which the
notices of confirmation apply. The more than 2,000 offers required will be made within the statutory ninety day period following the date of confirmation.
In addition to the market value of the property, which is to be calculated as of the date the notice of confirmation is registered and not the earlier notice of intention, an owner in occupation will also be paid for any costs or losses incidental to disturbance including moving to other premises. There is provision for compensating tenants and holders of security or mortgage interests, plus rules for other items and types of compensation. Of particular note is the right of an expropriated homeowner to claim additional compensation for the cost of relocating his residence in reasonably equivalent premises, if the compensation otherwise payable is not sufficient to permit this.
Many hon. members will also recall the strong support in the House of the provision in the new act whereby an owner may accept the government's offer of compensation and receive payment immediately, without prejudicing his right to claim additional compensation. An owner then has up to one year to negotiate settlement of such claims or to proceed in the Federal Court.
I should also point out that no resident will be required to move immediately. Obviously, the public examination of airport facilities announced last year and since reaffirmed, will help determine the timing and development of this airport.
In any event, it takes several years to develop an airport and thus many residents will not be required to move for a considerable period of time.
Clearly, it will be in the public interest to facilitate the continued residence of owners who wish to remain and this has also been the attitude of the Ontario government who are acquiring land in the adjoining area. Accordingly, such owners will be required to pay only the taxes and the usual costs of operation including maintenance and insurance, through to December 31, 1974.
In conclusion then, the decision to proceed has been made and I can assure the House that each owner will be dealt with compassionately and to the full extent of the new Expropriation Act.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank both the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) for providing copies of their statements in advance of the presentation and tabling of the respective statements in the House.
It is distressing that the government finds it necessary to confirm expropriations of some 18,000 acres of land involving over 2,000 property owners when the question of need for a second airport has not yet been determined.

subsubtopic: PICKERING TOWNSHIP SITE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO PROCEED WITH EXPROPRIATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PICKERING TOWNSHIP SITE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO PROCEED WITH EXPROPRIATIONS
speechtext: This is clearly locking the barn door after the horse has been stolen. Even if a second airport is needed, which many people seriously doubt, the decision today destroys any flexibility left in siting an airport which may not be put into use for a decade. Surely this is one of the worst examples of backward planning this country has ever seen.

subsubtopic: PICKERING TOWNSHIP SITE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO PROCEED WITH EXPROPRIATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PICKERING TOWNSHIP SITE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO PROCEED WITH EXPROPRIATIONS
speechtext:
The government says it is convinced of the need for a new Toronto airport. While it may have reports from its technical consultants, and even these have been conflicting from time to time, who has it consulted in the Toronto-centred region? At least 14 of the 22 successful metro Toronto candidates in the October 30 election went on record during the campaign as saying there was no proven need for a second airport. The Toronto city council executive committee, representing over 700,000 people, last Wednesday requested the abandonment of the expropriations prior to a public determination of need. The regional municipality of York, representing 166,000 people, and the township of Pickering, representing over 30,000 people, have made similar requests, as has the mayor of Scarborough. Most of the formal objectors at the expropriation hearings in November and December gave primary emphasis to the unanswered question of need.
Yet the government pushes blindly on with virtually no public consultation and confirms the Pickering expropriations.
The lengthy statement of the Minister of Transport or, at least, the first nine pages of that statement, can be boiled down to this. He is saying to the people of the Toronto-centred region: You need a second airport; we have decided. Yet in the last four pages it appears to have suddenly dawned upon the minister that he should be concerned about public participation. He is at long last prepared to honour the commitment of his predecessor and arrange for an independent group to hear representations from the public as well as from the provincial and municipal governments. This independent group is to determine the type and timing of the facilities required, and the people will be able to make inputs not only on the question of the airport but also as to the kind of urban region they want, and how this would affect air service and airports.
We welcome this opportunity for public participation. It is long overdue. But we find it impossible to believe that this government can in any way maintain an open mind on the question when it appears to have already made its decision. The expropriations which have been confirmed today are for an airport. They cannot be for any other purpose if they are to remain legally valid. The government knows this. How can the public participation proposed in these circumstances be anything but a charade? At best, this is political waffling to avoid the political impact of a decision already taken. The Minister of Transport says in his statement that this process will be the first of its kind and could be a model for the future. Expropriate now-determine need later. Heaven help us!

I would simply ask him, very seriously and very strongly, to consider making available to the proprietors of the property in that area the opportunity and the financial assistance necessary for them to obtain their own appraisers instead of having to depend merely upon the appraisers that the department will appoint. This invariably places the person who owns the home or land at a considerable disadvantage.
As to the decision itself, I cannot but agree with the very eloquent, very succinct and very excellent statement made by the hon. member for St. Paul's.

Perhaps, as he is a new member, he will not think me paternalistic for using those adjectives. I am really disturbed by the politics in the statement of the Minister of Transport. I am disturbed for a very fundamental reason. The Minister of Transport says very distinctly, as does the Minister of Public Works in his statement, that the government has decided (a) that a second

Toronto airport is needed, and (b) that Pickering shall be the location. Then he talks about public hearings after the expropriations are confirmed and he hints, but does not say, in referring to a public hearing that it is still possible for the government to change its mind. Mr. Speaker, I say earnestly to the minister that this is precisely the kind of cynical approach to participation by the people that degrades the value of government and the value of parliament.

subsubtopic: PICKERING TOWNSHIP SITE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO PROCEED WITH EXPROPRIATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PICKERING TOWNSHIP SITE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO PROCEED WITH EXPROPRIATIONS
speechtext:
If the government has made up its mind that there is need for a second airport and that Pickering should be the site, it ought to have the courage to say so and stand behind that decision, and not try to fool all the people in the Pickering area into thinking that the government can still change its mind.
I am not an expert in this field, Mr. Speaker, and do not claim to be. Personally, I am simply not convinced of the need for a second airport in the Toronto area. Indeed, I may be considered as not being willing to keep up with the times but I say without hesitation that I cannot convince myself of the value of ever bigger, ever faster, ever noisier aircraft in this country or in the world. I am not at all convinced that humanity will be better and happier if we can fly across the Atlantic or across Canada in one hour or two hours less time than we now can. It has seemed to me for a long time that human progress and the quality of human life are being sacrificed on the altar of bigness and speed in our present society. I am not at all persuaded that this is the way humanity ought to go or the direction in which the Canadian people ought to go.
If, however, a second airport is indeed needed, then I appreciate that no matter where you try to locate it there will be difficulties. My only difficulty with the statement made by the hon. member for St. Paul's is that he entirely avoided informing the House and the people of Canada that the Pickering site for the airport was chosen by the Ontario Conservative government, as well as by the federal Liberal government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his statement to the effect that the government intends to give notices of confirmations of expropriation, the Minister of Public Works points out that the decision involves Canadian communications and business.
He also mentions the effects on the quality of the environment in which people will have to live in that part of the country.
Obviously, the decision to confirm the expropriations is as important as the project itself. The government seems deeply concerned about all aspects of the program, and it expresses its intention to create an independant group to study those questions and hear the representations of the interested parties. We should rejoice in that initiative. Although this is an outstanding project which must be carried out, to my mind it is imperative that the persons chiefly concerned, namely those who will be expropriated, should have the opportunity to be heard.
We already know that many problems have arisen in connection with the expropriation in Saint-Eustache, precisely because the owners concerned have not always been treated as they had been promised they would be in regard to some very justified requests.
I have in mind certain complaints by many owners of land located at the end of runways of the Ancienne-Lorette airport, near land owned by the Department of Transport. People who would normally have sold land for home construction in the towns of L'Ancienne-Lorette and Sainte-Foy cannot do so because the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not finance the building of housing units in this area.
On page 10 in his statement on expropriation, the minister implies that everything is being looked after and that expropriated owners have nothing to fear because this expropriation will be carried out on the basis of a particular aspect in the act that says you must provide "a home for a home".
I also have in mind the expropriation, which goes back to 1967, of Valcartier Camp. It was carried out by the Liberal government. It was based on legislation very similar to the one mentioned earlier. People were forced to vacate the site. In certain case, threats were proffered, insinuating that they either had to accept the price offered or make a deposit of $5,000 before appealing to the court, which was quite false.
In other cases, Mr. Speaker, the people expropriated were promised jobs, which they never obtained since most of them are still standing in line at manpower centers just like all the other unemployed of this country.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. minister states that all those expropriated will be paid at market value; however, we cannot forget that inflation has not yet been curbed and that it is quite possible that some of those appropriated are farmers who own a small farm worth $40,000 where they manage to make a living, whereas in

January 30, 1973

five to six years such farmers, having given up their farm, will find themselves without jobs, owning only a house.
The hon. minister asserts that an effort will be made to preserve historical monuments and protect the natural beauties of the site.
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the hon. minister on all his good intentions. However, I hope the government will recognize that the major effort to be made is in the interest of preserving the dignity of citizens caught in this mesh.

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising on the third day of the present debate, I repeat the concern of many hon. members who think that we should not take so much of the time of the House in discussing this matter, particularly when there are important pending questions involving economic, social and welfare fields with which we must be deal. The government has not seen fit to bring these matters forward at the earliest possible moment. I hope there might be some disposition, perhaps later this day, to extend the sitting time on this debate in order that we might wind up the second reading stage and get on with other important matters that we have indicated previously we should like to see dealt with as a matter of priority.
One of the difficulties in this third series of debates in recent years on the question of capital punishment stems from the fact that the basis for debate has shifted to a substantial degree. I suggest we are no longer debating so much the abolition or partial abolition of capital punishment as the question of restoring capital punishment. Perhaps the distinction seems subtle. On reading the speeches made in the past two days of debate, one will note the suggestion implicitly or explicitly, that capital punishment to all intents and purposes has been abolished in this country. Factually that may be correct, although the statute providing for the death penalty is still in existence. If this bill passes, the death penalty will be retained for certain offences. However, I submit that the practice of the government over the past ten years has made it virtually impossible, except in very unusual circumstances, for capital punishment to be restored.
Personally, I am most disappointed at being forced once more to debate the question of partial abolition. As I said last night, this position satisfies no one. I believe we would be on much stronger ground if the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) had brought forward a straightforward measure asking for the total abolition of capital punishment. I think in that way we might have brought some legislative
Capital Punishment
resolution to this problem which would be more satisfactory than the solution we are likely to arrive at after the present series of debates has finished. Presumably, this question is to be studied in committee. I do not think that in this sort of debate we can really come to the heart of the problem.
In arguing for an extension of the present situation the Solicitor General suggested that, primarily, we do not have enough information. That argument has often been made in other cases and could be made in the present case. I think it will always be made. Certainly, in the next 10 or 20 years, or in the foreseeable future, there will not be available to us that kind of factual and convincing information that will convince all members of this House and of the general public that capital punishment either should or should not be abolished. The consideration of this question involves too many subjective elements. I do not think that Statistics Canada or the occasional social scientist can provide us with the kind of factual information that will clear away those doubts. We must accept this situation when considering capital punishment and remember that, certainly according to present practice, capital punishment has been abolished in this country. What we are really trying to do is formulate a law that will agree with the present practice.
From time to time people have questioned the government's right, legally or morally, to continue the practice of commuting death sentences. Not many doubt seriously that this activity will continue, or that it should. I presume that some segment of public opinion will argue that we should bring back the death penalty and give it effect. I hope in a few minutes to deal with the underlying causes for those requests for the return of capital punishment. I do not think such requests relate to increases in the murder rate. They reflect more a sense of apprehension, a sense of fear, if you like, and the knowledge, as one hon. member said last night, that the increasing wave of crime must be dealt with.
What are we talking about when we talk about this increasing wave of crime? No one has been specific. Are people talking about the rapidly rising cost of meat available at supermarkets? Are they talking of Bell Telephone's application for an increase in telephone rates, or about landlords who gouge tenants with rapidly rising rents? Or, are they talking about corporate welfare bums, to use the slogan the NDP leader used in his campaign, and their contribution to some unspecified kind of bureaucratic crime? Nobody has been specific as to what is meant by this wave of crime and wave of permissiveness that has engulfed society.
I feel that the question of capital punishment can be studied in an enlightened manner. There are areas of crime, too, which can be studied. Those areas are not to be mentioned facetiously, in the way I mentioned other so-called areas just now. For example, we know that during the past few years each and every year 5,000 Canadians have been killed on our highways. Over half these people have been killed directly or indirectly as a result of drunken driving. Drunk drivers are those who have reached the state of intoxication in which they cannot control their vehicle. These drunken drivers have driven on the high-

January 30, 1973
Capital Punishment
way and killed themselves or other innocent drivers or passengers who happened to be on those highways.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, to the best of my knowledge not one Canadian has ever been executed because he has been convicted on a murder charge arising out of drunken driving. Indeed, not only have we not executed any of these people who have killed their fellow citizens while under the influence of alcohol but many of them, after very moderate penalties, have gone on to drive and drink again. If we are concerned about the incidence of situations of this kind when thousands of our fellow citizens are being killed and maimed annually, maybe we should use the very obvious deterrent values some people argue for in connection with capital punishment to deal directly with a very real problem, that of the increase in deaths on the highways directly or indirectly caused by the abuse of alcohol.
Of course no one has seriously argued for that in this chamber, nor is anyone likely to do so.

speechtext:
I am the first one, as my colleague suggests, and I am not really suggesting it, Mr. Speaker, because I do not think it would be acceptable in any way, shape or form to the general public, nor would it be workable in any court of law.
There are a lot of things in terms of the wave of crime and the general permissiveness of society that have not been thoroughly looked at or analysed. If we are concerned about the increasing amount of violence in society, let us look at the roots of violence itself. Anyone who has spent any amount of time working with people who have run afoul of the law, whether in our courts or penitentiaries, has come away with the feeling that he has encountered a very sorry group of people. In most cases, these people come from homes that are almost non-existent or, to the extent that they are existent, are a very harmful influence on the individual. They come from backgrounds that would be recognized as producing these people who are emotionally, physically and socially deprived.
In our penitentiaries we are dealing with individuals who have not been able to cope with society for one reason or another, and who have often become distraught and desperate individuals. Perhaps nowhere is this more clear than in the latest preoccupation of our society with the very difficult offence of skyjacking. We are now beginning to get some clear feedback on the people involved in skyjacking activities. It is interesting to contemplate how our society is going to deal with people who hijack aircraft and take both planes and passengers on desperate journeys that indeed may end in death both for the skyjackers and some of the passengers. We are now finding that these people are the very last people in the world against whom we should consider invoking the death penalty, not because, as somebody might rush to suggest, they do not deserve it but simply because it would not be in the best interests of solving the very problem we are trying to resolve.
Here I quote a Dallas pyschiatrist, David Hubbard, who perhaps has examined, more exhaustively than any other

doctor, the individual make-up of skyjackers. In a recent interview on the CTV television network he said:
-one of the common threats of skyjackers as a group is their interest in suicide, only they don't want to shoot themselves; they want to manoeuvre society into the position where society will kill them. Then, they are not guilty of the sin of suicide, and they can go ahead and rise to heaven. So we give them a death, offer them the image, at any rate, of a death penalty.
What Dr. Hubbard is suggesting is that by instituting the suggestion of using the death penalty we, in effect, make it more difficult for us to deal with these often insane individuals. They are one example, one extreme group, of people with whom we are trying to deal in tackling the growing wave of crime.
How are we going to deal with people who are suffering internal, and often external persecution, who have become disoriented from society, filled with hostility and hate, and acting out of emotional passion that bears no relationship to their true status in society and to society's recognition of them? The escape of capital punishment, that they expect, will not in any way deter them. For them, it will almost be a release.
As I said a few minutes ago, Mr. Speaker, statistically speaking there is no final answer. In New Zealand, which is an interesting analogy for us in Canada, the death penalty was abolished just prior to World War II. Shortly thereafter the murder rate began to increase sharply. It peaked in the 1940's, and then decreased. A careful review of world statistics will show that the increase in the murder rate in New Zealand was commensurate with the general increase throughout the world, and that Canada's murder rate paralleled that of our sister dominion, New Zealand. It is, therefore, not by statistics that we will make any final decision on this question, but rather by trying to root out the causes for increased crime, increased lawlessness, and the growing evidence of harmful permissiveness in our society.
I detect as well the influence of the media in exposing us, not just on a daily but on an hourly basis, to crimes of base violence. I am not attributing any blame or sensationalism to the media, although perhaps that should be looked at in some more exhaustive context. But it is obvious when some bizarre act of violence occurs, such as took place recently in New Orleans, or some other sadistic act occurs, we have the facilities to see it now almost as it happens, in living colour, in our own homes. And when one is exposed to an event of this nature, although it may be happening 4,000 miles away in a city of one million, two million or 10 million people, and one sees it in one's living room, one may well think that it might be happening down the street on which we live, even though the most violent thing that happened to one on that street in the last ten years was to be hit on the back of the head with a snowball. Because we are so exposed to the mass media, we have to develop a new sense of sophistication, a new sense of detachment, particularly when we are exposed, in living colour, to the latest violent events that occur. If we do not develop that kind of tolerance and sophistication we may become almost crazed in our response.
If we are going to deal with the real roots and causes of violence, and with the real violence that exists in our society, we must be concerned with the over-all impact of violence rather than just the occasional but more limited
January 30, 1973

question of whether or not capital punishment, in terms of those who commit capital crimes, should apply. I think if we look at that question to any great degree we will have to come to the firm conclusion that we have not very effectively provided protection for society or rehabilitation for the offenders.
It is a shocking statistic that more than two-thirds of the people presently serving time in federal institutions, at great expense to the taxpayers, after their release will shortly commit further crimes and serve more time in those institutions. That is not good enough. It is not good enough in terms of society's protection, and it is not good enough in terms of the rehabilitation of the individual. Even on a very narrow basis, it is not good enough in terms of the millions of dollars spent annually to maintain those institutions. The difficulty has been that every reform and every change has occurred without sufficient understanding by or sufficient explanation to, the general public, and without those explanations and understandings it has been most difficult for society to understand and to accept possible improvements in our whole penal service.
Before us today, in addition to this partial abolition, there is the suggestion that we should think seriously about imposing a mandatory sentence of something like 25 years, and that no person convicted of the crimes suggested in Bill C-2 would be released before the end of that time. For the life of me, I cannot understand why that suggestion has any particular merit. Presumably the appeal in it is that there are people being released after such offences, and before 25 years have passed, who should not be released. To the extent that that is happening, Mr. Speaker, we must reject it. Indeed, we have to look at a situation in which no individual can be released into society without the likelihood of him being a responsible and law-abiding citizen. It is not just a question of a 25 year sentence because that may, in fact, be counterproductive. I think many officials who work with prisoners will tell you that in the life span of most men who spend time in institutions, there are times when they may be capable of being reformed and other times when they are not. To fix some kind of arbitrary figure would seem to me to destroy the very basis upon which, hopefully, our whole penal system is built.
I have on the order paper now a notice of motion, No. 27, which I would like the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and the government to consider very seriously. I should like the minister to indicate at some point whether this particular notice of motion, or one similar to it, might be acted upon in this session of parliament. My motion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should introduce a measure to establish a parliamentary committee to investigate all aspects of crime and its treatment in Canada, which should have specific terms of reference to closely examine (a) the subject of crime prevention and the work of the correctional consultation centre of the Solicitor General's department (b) the subject of punishment-its deterrent value and relevance to the rehabilitative process-with particular attention to capital punishment, by collecting factual information and holding public hearings (c) the correctional process, including the penitentiary and parole systems.
Capital Punishment
My purpose in suggesting this motion is that I think a fundamental requirement in dealing with the issue we are debating today, and the underlying questions related to it in terms of crime and punishment, is that we should have a well-educated public and a well informed House of Commons. I think the danger is that most of us tend to react to particularly violent events or perhaps news stories of one kind or another or, perhaps even more damaging, public opinion polls which really have little basis in fact.
Some people have already quoted the recent Weekend magazine poll. What value can a poll have when it sets out its case by showing a picture of a large noose with a ballot in the centre saying, "Which way will you vote?" I presume that poll was conducted everywhere except federal institutions but regardless of where it was conducted, out of subscribers numbering over two million, about 30,000 responded. I would not regard that response either as a fair sampling of public opinion or of the question being put.
I say, too, that the public has not been well informed from this point of view. There has grown a very large gulf between the leadership of known institutions, such as the various religious bodies, and those members of the general public who belong to the various churches. I have here a statement made by the Canadian Catholic Conference, the administrative body of the Roman Catholic church in Canada which reads in part:
We consider it an illegitimate use of the Bible, especially the Old Testament, to quote texts in order to argue, in our time, for the retention of the death penalty. Each biblical text supporting the death penalty must be studied in the light of its historical context, and not simply applied to present day Canada.
It goes on:
The question of the death penalty, in our opinion, ought not to focus on whether a convicted murderer, no matter how wanton, deserves to die. The focus should be on us: Should Canadians, as a community, try to break the escalating spiral of violence by refraining from violence even as a deterrent?
Mr. Speaker, I support the strong stand of the Canadian Catholic Conference and the other motions which have come from other major church bodies in this country urging that we totally abolish capital punishment. I would say that they also have a role to play in talking to their constituents, in exploring at greater length the underlying causes of this growing violence and the extent to which there may be indications of the real causes as well as the extent to which we are pursuing problems rather than solutions. It is important that we have committees similar to the ones I have outlined here. It is possible, when this bill gets into committee, that we will have the opportunity to examine other questions beyond the narrow one of the bill that the minister has introduced.
For my part, I would be strongly inclined, either at committee or report stage, to move an amendment to totally abolish capital punishment. I think we need to put that question to the test in the House now. I think it is becoming very farcical that we must come back here on a regular basis to partially abolish something that we had abolished over a decade ago.

January 30, 1973
Capital Punishment

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the highly controversial subject of the bill has been thoroughly and strongly discussed, and those who have dealt with it expressed contradictory opinions.
When this bill and its amendments will be put to the vote, each hon. member will have to assume his responsibilities as this will be a free vote even if there are some who maintain that is not so.
First, it is important to place the debate in its general present-day setting. We must at any cost break away from old and outdated notions of capital punishment, and resolutely place ourselves in the perspectives throwing light on the problem as it appears to us now.
It is imperative first to relinquish the old principles of retaliation, of payment of evil by evil, of retributive punishment. Ideas, morals as well as the need of the criminal policy have progressed with time.
It is therefore with a spirit adapted to the circumstances of our era that we should deal with the problem.
Therefore, it is not pointless to say that Canadian criminal law has achieved a great deal of progress in this matter. Should we not point out the effects of the 1961 legislation in this field? Capital punishment has since been abolished in the case of several kinds of murder. It remains applicable for capital murder. Even then the jury may, if they deem it justifiable, recommend clemency or pity. Furthermore, the 1961 act calls for an automatic review of cases by an appeal tribunal, especially in matters of law, proper proceedings and facts, and entitles the convicted person to appeal to the Supreme Court. Whether the murderer is rich or poor, his case can be brought before the highest court in the land without prior authorization.
Finally, no one under the age of 18 can be sentenced to death since 1961. It may be said that Canadian criminal law has been humanized in this field and that in practice capital punishment is meted out only for especially despicable crimes. As a result, the number of death sentences has decreased considerably since 1961. On looking over statistics given by the Department of Justice in the booklet on capital punishment, it may be seen that from 1961 to 1965, 34 persons were sentenced to death by Canadian courts which is an average of seven annually. From 1968 to 1972, six individuals were sentenced to death as a result of a five-year suspension of death penalty, except for the murder of police officers or prison guards.
Between 1920 and 1959, the average varied between 18 and 15.5 per year, while the Canadian population was less than at present.
In addition, as it can be noted, I only mentioned the convictions and not the executions, the number of which was still lower. As evidence, from 1962 to this day, there has been no execution.
This parenthesis on statistics enables us to conclude that today the death penalty is only imposed in Canada in unusual circumstances. We must therefore discuss the matter in realistic terms.
Surely the concept and finality of the death penalty has been altered. It is no longer a matter of punishing the criminal without regard for his rehabilitation, solely to serve as a terrifying example to his fellow-citizens. No matter how much opinions may vary on capital punishment, we all agree that whenever possible the delinquent must cease to be a menace to society through reform and not through his elimination, pure and simple. Whenever circumstances allow, the criminal must be reeducated and returned to society as a sociable member capable of coping with it, of being useful to it.
This having been said, the fact remains that some criminals cannot be changed, rehabilitated nor recuperated socially; they will always be a danger to the community.
It is from this point of view of real danger, of real necessity, that we must envisage capital punishment, that is, a radical end to the threat the criminal represents.
In this day and age, capital punishment must no longer be considered as the "supreme vengeance", but as a means of defence, an extreme means of protecting society. This then becomes a problem of "social protection" through the prevention of crime and, if need be, through the elimination of beings that are essentially antisocial and a constant menace to their fellow human beings.
Those who favour the abolition of the death penalty invoke many arguments, but I shall consider only a few.
First of all, some abolitionists claim that the state does not have the right to remove a citizen's life. Of course, this debate deals not only with the political concepts one may have about the state, but also with everyone's religious concepts.
Without going into a philosophical debate, let us say that in Canada nothing deprives the federal government of that power. According to the Constitution, criminal law falls within federal jurisdiction and, according to British North America Act section 91, parliament has the required authority to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada.
Thus, the government not only has the power but also the duty to see to publish welfare and to this end it should take all necessary steps to ensure the security of all citizens and to protect the life of innocent people.
A study of the problem in the context of the protection of society and the defence of the community shows that it is hardly possible to contest the state's right to definite elimination of dangerous individuals who are beyond rehabilitation.
In the case of some particularly heinous criminal, is it not the duty of the state to take all steps-the most radical, if required-to protect the rest of society and particularly the personnel of prisons and the other inmates? It is to spare the lives of penitentiary staff, of citizens in general and perhaps of certain members of the community, for instance, in case the criminal should escape, that the state must, in certain circumstances, eliminate an individual who is a constant menace to society.
Is it not this very duty of the state to protect public welfare, the security of the country, which leads to the outbreak of some wars?
(Mr. MacDonald (Egmont).J
January 30, 1973

How can we deny the state the right to take the life of a dangerous criminal while it has the right to demand of its citizens any sacrifice required for the survival of the community and the defence of the country?
The state can force soldiers to expose their lives to save their country. But why could it not resort to capital punishment in the same interest?
The duty to inflict death in certain cases does not run counter to morals anymore than the necessity to kill in times of war or in cases of self-defence. As a matter of fact, it is the self-defence of society and the protection of its components.
Second, Mr. Speaker, some abolitionists believe that capital punishment does not deter anybody from committing crime or has a weak effect of deterrence and that life imprisonment is as efficient.
In our society, Mr. Speaker, people feel differently as to whether capital punishment deters murderers. I do not think one can resort to statistics to support one's thesis whether for or against.
Statistics are subject to various interpretations; they are dubious. It is almost impossible to set a useful comparison between countries because of the differences in the legal definitions of crimes, practices of the public department and courts, methods used to gather crime statistics, moral and behavioural standards and, finally, political, economic and social conditions.
Those are data which cannot be assessed validly. Certainly, a rigid application of the death penalty does not prevent the commission of premeditated murders. The authors rely on their cunning to avoid either the police or being condemned due to a lack of sufficient evidence.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, they take so many precautions not to be uncovered. Caught in the act they kill the policemen trying to apprehend them. In the case of criminal procedures they do not hesitate to assassinate witnesses who would have them condemned. This shows that they are frightened by the idea of capital punishment. In fact, all penalties are exemplary. If we do not leave our cars along a curb where parking is prohibited it is because we are afraid of being ticketed. If the object of all penalties is to deter the delinquent-and they succeed to a large extent-by what miracle could the death penalty, which is the most rigorous of all, fail its purpose?
Perhaps it is difficult to establish the relationship between capital punishment and criminality; however, the idea of this extreme penalty remains certainly narrowly tied to certain savage and horrible crimes. This notion of the seriousness of the penalty has doubtless remained rooted in minds for generations and common sense tells us that no other risk than that of losing one's life could deter man from the criminal intent of committing murder.
Furthermore, the Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Capital Punishment stated in its report of 1956, and I quote:
They considered that it was particularly effective in deterring professional criminals from carrying weapons and committing crimes of violence. In addition, it was contended that abolition would endanger police because a criminal seeking to avoid arrest would have much less fear, of the consequences of the use of firearms or violence.
Capital Punishment
No doubt you will be told that it did not prevent police assassination, it happened recently in Toronto. But, in fact, the death penalty has not existed in Canada since 1962, the year the last death sentences were carried out.
My third argument relates to the execution of an innocent resulting from a judicial error which could entail capital punishment. The probability exists but it is far-remote and questionable. One cannot speak of conclusive cases, for it does not suffice to accuse oneself of a crime for which another person has been punished to conclude that the latter is innocent.
This was seen in Quebec with the Coffin case. If Simpson had died by assassination or by accident before retracting his confession we know how the abolitionists would have used this. Nobody would have dared express the slightest doubts on Coffin's innocence. In spite of this retractation are there not people who keep on believing in his innocence?
In connection with an eventual error this is what the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on capital punishment had to day on June 27, 1956 as recorded at section 60 page 60 of the white paper on capital punishment, and I quote:
Considerable emphasis was put on the risk of irrevocable error in capital convictions. The fact that there was no known Canadian instance of the execution of an innocent person indicated the effectiveness of present procedures by way of trial and executive review and this suggests that the risk of error does not present a reasonable argument for abolition in Canada.
Even when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) pointed out in 1966 that judicial errors did happen he mentioned the United States and England but not one case in Canada.
The alleged error can only take place in the accomplishment, by society, of a duty strongly demanded by the common good. Since this duty cannot be accomplished by individuals or social groups, there is no other choice for the public authority. I think law enforcement in Canada, as far as murder is concerned, does have the necessary safeguards for preventing an innocent from being put to death.
If this bill is passed by Parliament this will mean that we would extend for five years the law which was in force from December 29, 1967 to December 29, 1972. Several reasons are raised and, among others, that a longer period would provide further statistics.
Mr. Speaker, while I recognize that many people would like to see capital punishment abolished for ever, a greater number still are ready to accept it. This, of course stands from the aversion of the public for murder, "the crime of crimes". Traditionally the public has always associated capital punishment with this particular form of crime.
The abolition of any punishment held to be fair, efficient preventive, can only be recommended where it is clearly demonstrated that in the opinion of the ordinary citizen the punishment has not been really operative. Experience has shown that the abolition of capital punishment, at the time when the public at large is firmly in

January 30, 1973
Capital Punishment
favour of it, can create confusion and doubt with ensuing harmful repercussions on the administration of justice.
Mr. Speaker, at a time when the state has so much to do in its fight against crime, the accent should be put on protecting society rather than the criminal. There are reasons to believe that capital punishment can be a deterrent factor against armed robbery, and to abolish it at this time could only be interpreted by the masses of law breakers as a signal to engage in other criminal acts.
So, Mr. Speaker, for all the reasons I have stated, on second reading I will vote against Bill C-2, an Act to amend the Criminal Code, with regards to capital punishment, and vote for maintaining the law as it now stands.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, had it not been for the fact that the debate is to be continued for some time I would not have addressed the House on this subject having done so on two previous occasions.
I do not intend to repeat the arguments I raised in the two debates of 1966 and 1971. But I intend to place before the House the views of one who has had some experience with capital cases, not only from the point of view of the defence in court but also as prime minister-one who has had the ultimate responsibility, when a sentence of death has to be carried out, for signing the death warrant. Nothing gave me greater remorse than having to do this, and take the life of a fellow human being. That experience, I can tell hon. members this afternoon, equals the awfulness of having acted for an accused who was totally innocent, who was found guilty by a jury with a recommendation to mercy, and who was denied that mercy by the governor in council.
I do not know in how many cases I appeared for the defence but in writing down a list this morning, I arrived at 17 names from my recollection. Two of my clients went to the gallows; the others were acquitted. One of those individuals had his own views as to how the case should be conducted. I made it a point never to put the accused on the stand in murder cases because jurors did not hold it against an accused if he did not give evidence. Indeed, it was not until about 1900 that an accused in a murder case could take the stand and give evidence. I found that in cross-examination one could bring out the necessary facts upon which to build a defence, and I also ascertained by personal experience that when the death penalty was known to be the one to be exacted, jurors were very slow to convict. If there were any extenuating circumstances at all, the jury invariably found the accused not guilty. When there was any doubt at all, even doubt which had been conjured up, jurors tended to acquit.
This has been the history of capital cases for 300 years. When in earlier days not only were some offenders hung, but others were drawn and quartered, and others were disembowelled while they still lived, having been hanging for five or ten minutes, and allowed to see their bowels consumed by fire. Jurors would not convict. The result was that whereas in about 1800 there were some 200 different varieties of cases in which the death penalty could be imposed, with the passing years, jurors, repre-

senting the conscience of their nation invariably refused to convict.
I do not want to be repetitious but I told this story several years ago about a great grandfather of mine in York County. In the early 19th century executions were carried out in public. A lad of 17 was to be hung. The awful offence he had committed was pickpocketing. This was only 135 years ago. On the appointed day they gathered from all over the countryside. It was a day of celebration. Whisky was 90 cents a gallon. Everyone had a happy time. The lad mounted the gallows and following the custom made a speech to the assembled multitude pointing out that the wages of sin are death. And while he was awaiting execution, and while the execution was being proceeded with, four of the onlookers had their pockets picked. This gives one some idea of the deterrent value of capital punishment!
While I have not heard all the speeches made in this debate, I have been much impressed by the quality of those which have come to my notice. I must say to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) that since he assumed office as Solicitor General I have a great deal more hope that his department will be well-administered. I think his speech was one which deserved the widest circulation. It was the clear expression of a viewpoint which deserves the fullest consideration.
What I intend to do is simply to discuss some of the aspects of capital punishment and then place before this House the unusual anomaly, as I see it, created in consequence of the judgment of the Supreme Court of the United States in the Furman case. Their bill of rights having the same wording as the Canadian Bill of Rights, the judgment of that court will certainly receive serious consideration when the Canadian Bill of Rights is subject to interpretation on the question of murder, whether it be soon or later.
Last night I was thinking over this matter and decided to send a request this morning for the judgments of the United States Supreme Court. How many hon. members have actually studied those judgments? There has been a casual reference to them. I find, however, since the book containing the judgments is in the Library, that I am the first person to examine them. I will return to this in a moment because I think the judgment of that court has brought about, as a result of the arguments mobilized by the five judges, a state of mind among those in the judiciary and at the bar which may result in Canada putting an end to capital punishment.
I told the House a moment ago that there is nothing more trying for a Prime Minister than to sign the warrant of death. It worried me. It was my signature that sent the last two to the gallows in December of 1962. We in the cabinet at that time followed the course of examining in detail the evidence in the case as well as the recommendations not only of the Solicitor General but of the law officers of the Crown. Almost the first day after I became Prime Minister a capital punishment case came before the cabinet with a recommendation for mercy attached. The law officers said, as did the judge, that the sentence should be carried out. I made myself perfectly clear that I
January 30, 1973

felt that as long as I sat in the cabinet a recommendation for mercy would receive the full consideration and support of the cabinet in so far as determining whether or not there were extenuating circumstances.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, when the evidence was clear the law was carried out. If the law is wrong it must be changed by parliament, not by a cabinet.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
If you were to ask me why I felt so strongly about recommendations for mercy, I would say that, speaking from memory, I think there were 38 convictions with recommendations for mercy between 1930 and 1957 which were followed by execution.
Why was there a recommendation? In those days the jury was not allowed to know that they could make a recommendation for mercy. It meant that there was division. Finally, as the jury deliberated, the decision was arrived at in this way: "Well, I will go with you on a verdict of guilty provided you join a recommendation for mercy".
Let me go back to 1885 and the trial of Louis Riel. I have read all of the evidence in that case. Louis Riel appeared to have a perfect defence, that of being not guilty by reason of insanity. He had the best lawyers who could be procured for the defence, Lemieux and Greenshields, both of whom afterwards became chief justices in the province of Quebec. He received a recommendation for mercy.
I have often wondered how different the history of our country would have been if the decision made by the cabinet that I had the honour to be Prime Minister of had been carried out in his case. He carried an appeal forward to the Privy Council and it was based on whether or not stipendiary magistrate Richardson had properly charged the jury on the M'Naghten rules. The Privy Council held that it was a proper charge.
I mention that in passing, but I begin with the proposition: no execution where there is a recommendation for mercy. If it were otherwise, juries would say that they conclude there is no purpose in recommending mercy and, regardless of the evidence, if there were any doubt they would acquit. That is all very fine when you are appearing for the defence, but I am not saying that it always leads to justice, even though I was one who always endeavoured to defend those who were innocent.
Let me tell the House about one of the greatest lawyers for the defence that Britain ever produced, Sir Norman Birkett. My hon. friend from Toronto who spoke yesterday was present on the occasion when I introduced Sir Norman Birkett, who afterwards became Lord Chief Justice. He had a tremendous personality. In introducing him I went a little farther than I should and said that he was the greatest defender of murderers in all British history. He resented that; he said it was a frightful statement to make. He defended 49 people who had been charged with murder and none had been convicted, he was not quite right; he had forgotten the first one.
There is no equality among individuals who are charged with murder. For example, you do not hear of many wealthy men going to the gallows. The hon. member for
Capital Punishment
Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) made some mention this afternoon of social background and the like. I had my own feelings about this at the bar. Although only five per cent of my practice dealt with criminal cases, I made a rule early on that however poor a person was, in the British tradition I would defend him and go through to the Supreme Court if necessary, regardless of fee. That is the only way that justice can be assured. Because if justice has to be bought by securing outstanding counsel, then one of the most serious elements in capital punishment will have been achieved, namely that it is much easier for a wealthy man to go through an open gate than it is for a poor man.
May I mention another matter, Mr. Speaker? This is a free vote, but what does that mean? It means that each one of us according to his or her conscience will determine the course. But there is something wrong with this so-called debate, for the first principle is that the Cabinet shall say what it believes on a free vote. That is a prerequisite. Who speaks for the government over there?
Oh, no! The hon. gentleman points to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). He speaks for himself but not for the entire cabinet, unless the hon. gentleman is able to tell me that what the Solicitor General says represents the viewpoint of the Cabinet and the Cabinet will vote as the Solicitor General votes. Have I that assurance? The answer is silence from the gentleman.
I say that the constitutional principle is that the government must state its view. Let me quote from what happened in the United Kingdom in 1956 when the then Lord Chancellor, Lord Kilmuir, stated:
Her Majesty's Government are clearly and unequivocally of the view that capital punishment must be retained. I endorse fully today what my right hon. and gallant friend the Home Secretary has said in another place about the dangers of this bill. However, I have said that this will be a free vote and I do not withdraw from that statement in any way. The government do not expect or wish that any noble lord should speak or vote against this bill out of a sense of loyalty to the government and least of all from party feeling. At the same time no government with any sense of responsibility could abstain from expressing their view on such an important matter.
We do not have that. Where are they and where do they stand? What is their view? Whatever their stand is they should stand together. That is the principle of constitutional government. Why is that not being followed?
My next point is this. An hon. member asked me a few moments ago in private conversation whether I believed that a member should vote regardless of any consideration other than his conscience, and my answer was no. Some hon. members say they are going to vote for this bill to retain a form of selective capital punishment although they, in their hearts, believe it is wrong. Surely, mankind had an example of that with Pontius Pilate. How can you take a stand in your heart in favour of something and then vote the other way? On a free vote everyone should let his conscience be his guide. I used to say to juries: In the panoply of this place, surrounded by something entirely new to you, I do not want you to agree with the view I express because I am prejudiced in favour of the accused. I am not on the jury and my learned friend the Crown prosecutor is not on the jury either. Then, I would

always say: His Lordship is not on the jury either. There are not 13 members of the jury. Some judges did not like that.
Each one of you in this House has the conscientious responsibility of voting according to your conscience and for no other reason. Somebody will say that his constituents feel otherwise. I have never been able to find out what my constituents thought, except in a general way. I know that even the government was fooled on October 30. Whenever I have taken a stand that my constituents did not believe in, they never held it against me. Constituents have never held this against any other member that I know of, providing the stand being taken was a conscientious one.
Some members are in a quandary to know what to do because they have had petitions. I do not know whether you have had anything to do with petitions, but I suggest you can get people to sign anything. One of the finest examples of this took place in Madison, Wisconsin, about 15 years ago when members of a university decided they would find out what form of petition they could get signed. They put in the petition that they opposed everything in the Bill of Rights including "a", "b", "c", "d", and "e", and they got 3,000 signers on streets. People will sign any kind of petition.
Do you vote according to a petition? I am not going to repeat what has already been said, but the greatest lesson was ever given on parliamentary government and what members should do was given in that famous speech of 1774 by Edmund Burke. I will quote only a few lines, but it is well worth sending to the library to get the whole thing. He said:
Certainly, gentlemen, it ought to be the happiness and glory of a representative to live in the strictest union, the closest correspondence, and the more unreserved communication with his constituents. Their wishes ought to have great weight with him; their opinion high respect; their business unremitted attention.
He went on to state:
But his unbiased opinion, his mature judgment, his enlightened conscience, he ought not to sacrifice to you-to any man, or to any set of men living.
That is the essence of being a Member of Parliament. The electors do not send Members of Parliament here to be delegates. They do not send them here for the purpose of being automatons. They send them here as Members of Parliament because they believe in general that the individual in question is of mature judgment and able to form appropriate conclusions.
One Prime Minister was once asked what his idea of leadership was, and he said that if you compare the electorate to sheep and there are two gates in the corral and you want them to go out one gate but they do not go that way but go through the other gate, you get ahead of them because you are their leader. That is not the kind of representation that makes for good parliament or the great institution of parliament. I am not going to labour that any further.
Why is there this feeling among people concerning the high degree of law breaking in this nation, in the United States and in the United Kingdom? Why is it that in 1970 the number of criminal offences in Canada amounted to 1,103,504 and with a population of 22 million in 1971 it

amounted to 1,186,252? In other words, about 5 per cent of the Canadian population has been committing offences, not against the vehicles act, federal statutes, other than the criminal code, or against provincial laws, but actual criminal offences. Why is there this permissiveness? Is there any danger today for a person committing a crime in this country?
It was my government that set up the parole board and I should be the last to criticize any of its activities. But, Sir, the parole board ought not to be a freedom board for individuals who have been convicted of serious offences.

Now, I come to another phase. I don't know how many of you have studied the judgment in the Furman case, given by the Supreme court of the United States. It is a long judgment, and was rendered on June 29 last. The case before the Supreme Court involved three men, one who had committed a horrible murder, and two who had committed frightful rape. They appealed, and they contended that under the Bill of Rights of the United States the death penalty could no longer be imposed.
The Supreme Court judges heard the appeal, and the basis for quashing the sentence of death in each of the cases was the interpretation given by the majority of the court to the expression in the U.S. Bill of Rights which decrees that "cruel and unusual punishment" shall not be imposed. The wording in the American Bill of Rights is almost identical with that in the Canadian Bill of Rights. The Canadian Bill of Rights provides:
Every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an Act of the Parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian Bill of Rights, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment of infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized and declared, and in particular, no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to ... impose or authorize the imposition of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment-
At once the argument was raised in the Supreme Court that hanging, electrocution, or death in the gas chamber was a practice that had been followed for long years. The question was asked: how could it be a cruel and unusual punishment? I cannot read the judgments of the judges at length, but I ask hon. members to read them because they have a message for Canada. Mr. Justice White used these words:
To arrive at the conclusion that the death penalty violates the Eighth Amendment-
That is the amendment to the U.S. constitution which states that cruel and unusual punishment shall not be imposed.
-we have had to engage in a long and tedious journey. The amount of information which we have assembled and sorted is enormous. Yet, X firmly believe that we have not deviated in the slightest from the principles with which we began.
The next words are very significant because they apply to our country as well.
At a time in our history when the streets of the nation's cities inspire fear and despair, rather than pride and hope, it is difficult to maintain objectivity and concern for our fellow citizens. But the measure of a country's greatness is its ability to maintain compassion in time of crisis. No nation in the recorded history of man has a greater tradition of revering justice and fair treatment for all its citizens in times of turmoil, confusion, and tension than ours. This
is a country which stands tallest in troubled times, a country that clings to fundamental principles, cherishes its constitutional heritage, and rejects simple solutions that compromise the values which lie at the roots of our democratic system.
Naturally, I don't say that I accept that description of the United States. It is more in keeping with a description of the United Kingdom, the giver and the fountain of common law which today is part of the history of the United States. Then, there follow these words:
In striking down capital punishment, this Court does not malign our system of government. On the contrary, it pays homage to it. Only in a free society could right triumph in difficult times, and could civilization record its magnificent advancement.
In recognizing the humanity of our fellow beings, we pay ourselves the highest tribute. We achieve "a major milestone in the long road up from barbarism" and join the approximately 70 other jurisdictions in the world which celebrate their regard for civilization and humanity by shunning capital punishment.

There is but one conclusion that can be drawn from all of this- i.e., the death penalty is an excessive and unnecessary punishment which violates the eighth amendment. The statistical evidence is not convincing beyond all doubt, but it is persuasive. It is not improper at this point to take judicial notice of the fact that for more than 200 years men have laboured to demonstrate that capital punishment serves no purpose that life imprisonment could not serve equally as well. And they have done so with great success. Little if any evidence has been adduced to prove the contrary. The point has now been reached at which deference to the legislatures is tantamount to abdication of our judicial roles as factfinders, judges, and ultimate arbiters of the constitution. We know that at some point the presumption of constitutionality accorded legislative acts gives way to a realistic assessment of those acts ... We have this evidence before us now. There is no rational basis for concluding that capital punishment is not excessive. It therefore violates the eighth amendment.
When I read that some members say the deterrent value is tremendous I wonder whether they have studied the report that was produced by the United Nations committee which was representative of all the nations of the United Nations at the time. That committee studied capital punishment and found as follows:
... it is generally agreed between the retentionists and abolitionists, whatever their opinions about the validity of comparative studies of deterrence, that the data which now exist show no correlation between the existence of capital punishment and lower rates of capital crime.
Now, what does Sellin say? The following is quoted in one of the judgments in this case:
Sellin's statistics demonstrate that there is no correlation between the murder rate and the presence or absence of the capital sanction. He compares states that have similar characteristics and finds that irrespective of their position on capital punishment, they have similar murder rates. In the New England States, for example, there is no correlation between executions and homicide rates. The same is true for mid-western states and for all others studied. Both the United Nations and Great Britain have acknowledged the validity of Sellin's statistics.
This is a judge who served ten years in the criminal courts, and then as a judge particularly concerned with criminal malters. At another point in the judgment he said:
