subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PUBLIC REPORTS OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent looked surprised when you called him.
In introducing this bill, I am well aware of the usual fate of private members' public bills, especially those introduced by opposition members. They are usually discussed at length for the full hour. More often than not, speakers from the government benches express their approval of the principles of the bill, but then proceed to talk it out and refuse to allow a vote to be taken. I realize that this is probably an integral part of our procedure. It is the government's responsibility to initiate legislation in the first instance. I suppose the corollary of this is that it is also the government's position that they should not accept suggestions from the opposition. However, how many times do we hear government members chide us for being critical, but not constructive? Yet, when we do propose, they invariably oppose.
Surely, there are certain areas which should be nonpolitical. Surely, there are areas involving the public interest which can be discussed on a non-partisan basis and surely the whole question of the safety of public transportation, whether it be by land, sea or air, is so vital that it should be open to complete and frank scrutiny. This bill, through minor amendments to the Railway Act, would go a long way toward lifting much of the secrecy which surrounds the increasing number of accidents on our Canadian railways. The bill proposes to make an amendment which would alter only one word in section 226(1) of the Railway Act. The present section reads "The Commission may appoint". This bill would change the word "may" to "shall". In other words, it would make the commission's responsibility in this regard mandatory instead of permissive, as at present.
The section of the Railway Act which would be amended by this bill implies a duty upon the Canadian Transport Commission, not only to investigate accidents after they have happened, but to investigate railway running conditions and operating conditions with the object of preventing accidents. This section of the act places this duty on the commission. The commission should not wait for an accident to happen. If there is a deterioration of running equipment, of a road bed, or if the railways are not carrying out proper inspections and safety procedures, the CTC should step in and see that these conditions are corrected.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PUBLIC REPORTS OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PUBLIC REPORTS OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
In my dealings with the CTC, I found that there was a continual contest between the CTC, the public and the railways. The CTC absolved itself of any responsibility by saying that under the act they do not have to investigate these cases. My bill attempts to correct this situation which exists today. It is very detrimental to the public interest, to those who use the railways and must be very disturbing to those who operate them.
After an inquiry has been made by the commission, under the present act, there is no compulsion to make the result public. Bill C-ll would amend section 226(2) by adding a clause which would force the commission to make available to the public the results of all inquiries

they have made into running conditions, safety conditions, road conditions as well as inquiries into accidents that have occurred. This, briefly, is the gist of what my bill proposes to do.
In case there is any question as to why I consider the whole matter of railway safety important, I wish to quote from some authorities. I quote from page 8 of The Third Annual Report of the Canadian Transport Commission 1969:
There have been many technological advances in the railway industry during the last decade, leading to greater operational efficiency, but these have created new safety problems. The increase in efficiency has not been matched by any significant decline in accident rates.
You can project that statement and say that if there has been no decline, then there obviously must have been an increase. I now wish to quote from the Fourth Annual Report of the Canadian Transport Commission 1970, page 9:
In its 1969 report the commission referred to the safety problems being created by technological advances in the railway industry. It indicated a special program had been started to identify such problems and determine methods of solving them.
During the first half of 1970 the commission became concerned by the increase in the number of accidents on the railways.
The report goes on to state that, as a result, a special inquiry was conducted into certain accidents in Quebec and was later expanded to deal generally with railway maintenance and operation practices:
"and all matters and things likely to cause or prevent railway derailments and collisions between trains."
The report was completed and made public. A service to Canadians was performed by making the details of the report public.
The second investigation referred to is the Jones Report, the report which Mr. D. H. Jones, the Chairman of the Railway Transport Committee, was commissioned to undertake. This report was presented last year. While it was quite thorough, frankly, along with many other members of parliament I was disappointed with many of its conclusions. I do not think it solved anything. In fact, it simply delayed a final solution by suggesting that a tripartite committee be set up to carry out further investigation. So, the report did not solve anything. Nevertheless, that is not the crux of my position. My position is that, regardless of the recommendations in this report, there has been no change in the situation. The public is still not being made aware of what is going on in railway operations. No attempt has been made to open up this area to the public or to explain what is causing these accidents.
I do not pretend that this bill of mine is original. In the last parliament, the then member for Moose Jaw introduced a somewhat similar measure. His went further than mine does; he would have placed more onus on the railway operating people to make reports. But the purpose of the bill was the same-to lift some of the secrecy attaching to railway operating conditions and railway accidents. That bill received a sympathetic hearing. All the members who spoke on it said they were strongly in favour of the principle and that we would be doing a public service by allowing the public access to reports on running condi-
January 30,1973

tions and causes of accidents. But like all private bills this one, too, was talked out and nothing happened.
One would have hoped that following the initiative taken by the hon. member, somewhere along the line the government itself would have introduced legislation to have improved the situation, especially in view of the fact that the Canadian Transport Commission has openly admitted that the present situation is unsatisfactory. But instead of the situation being any clearer than it was previously, the public, today, is completely at sea. We hear stories about accidents being caused as a result of defective maintenance of the running bed, because the size of inspection crews has been cut down in the interest of economy, and so on. We hear stories of accidents being caused by faulty equipment, machinery which has not been properly inspected. All these things are disturbing to the public. The situation must be a frustrating one for the railways, too, because much of the blame for these accidents is being placed at the door of the companies. I believe it is in the interests of both the public and of the railways that investigations should be made and that the results of the investigations should be made public.
In the debate on the bill introduced by the former member for Moose Jaw, mention was made of privileged communications between the companies, their employees and others. I admit that some of this correspondence may be privileged, but I do not think we ought to sweep everything under the rug, saying it is not in the interests of the public that this information should be divulged. This is not the attitude taken toward other modes of transportation. In the case of air transport, for instance, accidents are inquired into and details are made public. The public is informed, for example, whether an accident has been caused by pilot error or by equipment failure. Everything is divulged. The same thing happens if there is a tragedy at sea. I cannot see why a distinction should be made in this area between rail travel and other forms of travel.
The United States has adopted a policy which is much more in the public interest. Under the United States transportation act of 1966, which was passed at about the same time as our own transportation act, a transportation safety board was set up. The sole purpose of this board, as I understand it, is to investigate causes of accidents and to make reports so that the public may know what has happened. Contrast this with the situation in Canada. It is true the CTC has power to make inquiries, but I defy any member here to get the results-to get any details of those inquiries. I have attended several committee meetings at which the Chairman of the CTC, on top-ranking officials of that body, have been present. Just try to pry out of these men details of what happened in a particular accident. One committee member, in frustration last year, said it was like trying to nail jelly to a wall. All you get is a discussion of legalities. Under the law, they say, we are only charged with doing so much. You gentlemen are Members of Parliament. You know the law. Why ask as? I say that we, as Members of Parliament, are entitled to know what is going on.
Railway transportation is a mode of transport subsidized directly by the Canadian people. We are shareholders. We are users. We have a right to know that the railways are being operated in such a way that the safety
The Railway Act
of those who use the lines is secured. Under the present system the only chance we have of getting information from the CTC is to question officials when they are here before the committee. Even then, instead of straight answers we get fencing and dancing and dodging. Either those officials do not want to answer, or they do not have the answers ready. I recommend that the House let this bill go to a committee where members would have an opportunity to investigate all aspects of railway safety and come up with workable solutions to protect the interests of the public.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PUBLIC REPORTS OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) for having brought this bill to the attention of all Members of Parliament. I support this attempt to get the railways of this country, whether publicly or privately owned, to disclose details of accidents which occur on the railway system. Though we shall undoubtedly hear speeches from across the way to the effect that there is considerable merit in what the hon. member proposes with respect to public disclosure of circumstances surrounding accidents on railways, there will be less readiness to take the necessary action to have the bill sent to committee. I believe all members over there, including the minister in charge of urban affairs, should allow the bill to pass and go to committee, so that instead of merely talking about the situation we could get things done.
I am sure the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) is aware that, since the election, parliament has emerged as a far more significant body than it was last year when initiative rested entirely in the hands of the cabinet. In these circumstances, it should be far more responsive to the desires of individual members.
The hon. member for Moncton has introduced a bill which, in my view, is of considerable importance and I wish to deal with it, if I may, from the point of view of one who comes from the Prairies. In my area of Assiniboia, if you drive between the two major urban centres-if I may call them that-from the city of Weyburn to the town of Assiniboia, you can cross six railroad crossings. There was a series of accidents on these crossings last summer. These accidents were of real significance to the question of area transportation. One accident happened in the middle of the night when a pair of individuals driving a truck were hit by a train. Apparently these two were not used to the particular highway and were unaware of the peculiar way in which the rail lines crossed the highway, which was at a certain angle that made it almost impossible to see the train. That was a major accident. In addition, we have had at least two derailments in that area.
I suspect that if there were some kind of public disclosure made of the cause of derailments in the Assiniboia area, you would find the railway companies were not maintaining to the required standard the beddings and the track. You would find that the cause of the accidents was that the railroads had not lived up to their responsibility in a part of the country from which they have drawn considerable revenue from the land they obtained when the railroad was put through, from the mineral rights in the area, and from many other sources. The tracks in that

January 30, 1973
The Railway Act
area are not up to the standard required for moving grain, and railroaders should not have to work on them.
My father worked the rails, as did my grandfather and many others in Saskatchewan and on the Prairies. They can tell you all about travelling on those lines. Public disclosure of the causes of accidents would be one way to gain information that would enable us to improve the lines and the service on those lines. In this way, those who work on the lines would be provided with some element of safety. These railroaders can tell you all about their attempts to book off because they did not want to travel those lines.
During the election campaign I did some travelling between two towns in my area. I remember watching, with a constituent of mine a train going over the tracks and seeing the movement of the tracks. They were moving as much as eight to ten inches as the train went over them. I contend that, in the event of an accident on that track, there should be public disclosure of the condition of the track. I and the people of Assiniboia know why the railroad is leaving the track in such a condition. It is because there are 605 miles of track they want to abandon in that area. However, that is not the subject of this particular debate.
I believe the hon. member's private bill is a very good one and that we should accept it, knowing full well its significance. There have been some tragic accidents on railway crossings. There was one in Quebec, I believe it was, involving a group of young people, some of whom were killed and others injured when their bus was hit by a train. There are other examples in my area where people in cars have been hit by trains at railway crossings as have people in trucks. This underlines the fact that there is a real need for reform in the area of public safety on the railroads, and that action ought to be taken by the Canadian Transport Commission. The first action that should be taken is that the chairman should be fired. Then, we could go on from there and bring in some measures relating to public safety.
At certain times of the day in my constituency it is absolutely impossible to tell whether a train is coming along the tracks or not, and I have to cross these tracks all too often. The safest drivers who cross the tracks are bus drivers who bring their vehicles to a halt. Other people are insane if they go over the crossings at 10 or 15 miles an hour.
Many constituents have written to me about the threat posed by boxcars or flatcars going along the tracks. For example, at crossings there are no warning signals. If flatcars are moving along the track at night, then you cannot pick them out with your headlights when you come to a crossing, and as a result many accidents are caused. This is why the question of public safety is of great importance. I suggest one of the first moves to improve public safety would be to pass this private member's bill thus enabling public disclosure to be made of railroad accidents.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PUBLIC REPORTS OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I stood up a couple of weeks ago to make my maiden speech I referred to that strip of the country known as the green belt, or mid-Canada. I talked about the great dis-

tances we travel across the country and I spoke briefly about the way in which the railroads are failing us. Canada is a country that is tremendously dependent upon the railroads. There are two major railroads in this country which in my opinion, really do not want to run a railroad at all. Let me qualify that. One railroad, the CPR, has no interest in running a railroad, in my opinion. The other railroad, the CNR, plays a secondary role. But fundamentally neither is interested in running a railroad in this country in any modern sense.
There is a debate raging throughout the country about whether or not there should be a pipeline down the Mackenzie to satisfy the demand for oil and gas. Some hon. members have suggested that the railroads should look at ways in which they can contribute to the development of a new kind of ground transportation to compliment this kind of activity. But the railroads are just not interested. If a similar opportunity were offered to some other industry, it would be eager to grab it. There has been talk about developing an alternate means of ground transportation to the building of the new airport at Pickering. Where are the aggressive railroads who should seize this opportunity and develop ground transportation as the alternative? I believe we are approaching a major crisis in terms of growth and demand for energy, and that the railroads of this country will have to play a role.
I have lived in northwest Ontario for many years, in the town of Rainy River, which was a railroad town. I saw what happened to the people of that community when overnight the railroads decided to pull out-not completely but just about. They turned to diesel power and laid off 100 people, which practically wiped out any real estate values in that community.
The relationship that exists between the railroads and their employees is one that just cannot be imagined. I have heard railroaders say: "We don't work for the railroad but for the union; how the roads run, we just don't know". Employees who have worked for 35 years for the -CNR in one case, and who have worked 42 years for the CPR in another case, have found a carbon copy of a letter on their desks stating that they had been laid off effective the day before. The people who live in the north country and in the greenbelt are dependent upon the railroads, yet the railroads take these arbitrary decisions. It is enough to make the people in that area lose faith in Canada and make them wonder whether we are interested in solving our problems.
Early in December the CPR announced that they were going to lay off 22 operators between Thunder Bay and Winnipeg, and that in their place service centres would be set up. Apparently the CTC agreed to this. We have had some experience with the service centre at Thunder Bay. I have pictures of the service centre in the old city of Port Arthur, which I will show hon. members if they want to see them. These pictures show plaster falling off the ceilings, washrooms in dirty condition and so on. Those are the so-called service centres. These 22 men are going to be laid off. It is said they will be picked up in some other area, but somewhere along the line somebody will be bumped.
January 30, 1973

The name of the game, as far as the railroads are concerned, is subsidy. They go to the CTC, which allows them to lay these people off and run the railroads and services by using Zenith numbers, and so on. But the people are not going to ride these railroads. A year from now they will be back before the CTC saying the business is not there and they need bigger subsidies. The name of the game is not running a railroad, it is getting subsidies.
I support in general the implications of this bill because railroad safety is a subject that has bothered us a great deal. I have not the exact figures with me this afternoon, but I would suggest in the last 10 or 15 years the number of section men has been reduced to about 20 per cent or 25 per cent of what it used to be.
Last year, between April 20 and June 1, there were ten serious accidents on the railroad in the area between Thunder Bay and Sioux Lookout, and east, alone. On April 20 there was a derailment at Sunstrum with two lives lost and eight persons injured. I do not have the exact dates, but there was a derailment at Kelly, on the Sioux Lookout line, with 23 cars derailed and 11 persons sent to hospital. There was a derailment at Parmachenne, east of Thunder Bay, with a damaged bridge. There was a derailment at Jelly, seven miles west of the Neebing yards. There was a derailment near Shabaqua, 43 miles west of Neebing. There was a derailment between Garda and Arrita, about 30 miles west of Neebing. There was a derailment between mileage 78 and 79 on the Fort Frances subdivision.
There were also three bridges damaged, a washout near Griff on the Sioux Lookout line and a bridge damaged at mileage 20.8 on the Sioux Lookout line. There was a bridge damaged by fire west of Quetico, at mileage 109.6. There was another bridge accident subsequent to this which caused a great deal of damage, but the railway company has not cleaned up the pollution which resulted. These ten separate accidents happened between April 20 and June 1. In the north country we are now approaching the spring thaw, at which time washouts and accidents occur.
I am please^ to have an opportunity to speak on this matter because it is time we warned the railroads that we will be watching for accidents that may occur. I hope in our area there is not a repetition of what happened last year. Many of the employees are disturbed about this situation and fear for their lives.
Let me conclude by saying that an aggressive and concerned railway industry is vital to Canada, Canadian unity, progress and, in days of growing energy shortages, probably to Canadian survival. This industry must be vitally concerned with its responsibilities for the safety and the welfare of employees. If the management of the railways, particularly the CPR, does not want to assume responsibility, perhaps it is time parliament saw to it that management of these companies in Canada is put in other hands.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PUBLIC REPORTS OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in support of the hon. member's private bill. As hon. members who have been here for some time are aware, every year Members of Parliament
The Railway Act
in all parties raise this and other issues concerning various aspects of our railroad system. Every year in this House and before the transport committee the same issues are raised. The hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas), who has been here longer than me, can probably vouch for this. In spite of that fact, nothing seems to be done. I am getting sick and tired of government members saying the same things, with the same result. It is time for us to quit talking a good fight.
The whole matter of making public the results of inquiries into rail mishaps has been aired time and again in this House. The former member for Moose Jaw, Mr. Skoberg, raised this issue repeatedly. I have a file of press releases, correspondence with the Canadian Transport Commission, railway union officials and officials of the railways all concerning the safety of operation. Any amendment to Canadian railway legislation which will do something about this and other matters will be welcomed. I suggest it is long overdue as far as we in this group are concerned. We must do a lot more to restore public confidence in the safety of rail transportation. This mode of transportation usually has the best safety record, but confidence is disappearing.
I suspect that many of those who have worked on the railroads since I left will tell you that many accidents can be attributed to a decrease in the number of train inspectors, car inspectors and track maintenance personnel. I do not understand how a track can be properly inspected by a crew driving in a truck along a highway parallel to the track. No one can convince me that this is proper track inspection or maintenance, but both companies have been getting away with this practice for a number of years. The rate of railway mishaps, I suggest, has increased in almost direct proportion to the decrease in the number of maintenance personnel.
I can never understand why the results of inquiries into rail mishaps are not made public. I can only assume it is because of fear. I recall the tragedy of the crash of a DC-8 aircraft in Toronto a couple of years ago. The report of that inquiry was made public and every member of this House received a copy. This report even gave in detail the last conversations of the aircrew with the control tower before the crash. Every detail of that inquiry was made public, but nobody was looking for revenge or anything else; no one was looking for a scapegoat.
The public needs and has the right to know the results of these inquiries. Surely this applies to rail transportation just as it applies to air traffic. The hon. member for Moncton and others, including the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner), have been making efforts in this area for a number of years. I imagine we will be members of the transport committee again during this parliament, and I suggest that we get together to find more effective ways, as we have in respect of other issues, to get results.
If government members choose to talk out this bill we can take the matter up again before the transport committee. But it would be nice if the House gave this bill second reading and referred it to the committee; we could then deal with it when we meet with officials of the Canadian National system and study their annual report. This would provide an occasion which we have not had for a

January 30,1973
The Railway Act
good many years to question the officials of the Canadian Pacific. Too often CNR officials are the only ones required to appear before a committee of this House. The CPR, which I submit has an even worse record, never has to come before the committee and give an accounting of the discharge of its responsibilities to the public under the Railway Act.
It would be nice if this bill were to be given second reading in a few minutes. I hope the hon. member for London East will agree. There would be no problem in reading this bill the second time. It may not go beyond that stage because the government may want to amend the Railway Act; and God bless it if it does! It would be useful from the standpoint of the work of the transport committee if this bill were given second reading now. We could then deal with it and meet with officials of the Canadian National Railways; officials of the CPR could also appear. Let us pass the bill; this measure is long overdue.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) who is a good friend of mine and is the sponsor of Bill C-ll, an act to amend the Railway Act. I think his bill should be placed on the statute books of this country.
Prior to my election in 1968 I was a CNR railway engineer, a head end man. Between 1941 and 1968, 27 years, I worked in that capacity. For the first ten years I worked as a fireman and for the next 17 as an engineer running yard, freight and passenger trains in southwestern Ontario.
Railways conduct their own investigations, as does the CTC. In the case of crossing accidents a "slow" order is placed on the crossing where a person has been killed until the accident has been investigated by a CTC investigator. I think statistics will show that most of the people killed by a moving train at a crossing lived within 25 miles of the crossing. They knew it was there and perhaps crossed it every day on their way to and from work.
The adage stop, look and listen means nothing to some people. Wigwags and flashers mean nothing. To some, flagmen mean nothing. I know of flagmen who have been run down by motorists at crossings. And let us remember the number of people who are killed in automobiles through running into trains stopped at crossings. Some drivers will even race a train to the crossing, and when they beat it they will turn around and thumb their nose at you. For many months I ran a train between London and Windsor. One fellow used to haul fruit and vegetables to the Windsor market. He played this game with us for about five weeks. Then one morning at a quarter to five we nailed him, and that was it.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the railways are trying out a new system for the care and maintenance of railway equipment and track. Five men used to look after approximately ten miles of track; today they look after 30 miles of track and others operate as part of a gang that works out of a bus. Many of these employees who are personal friends of mine will tell you that even if they had the

supplies necessary for looking after all the track, it would be impossible to do so because there are no longer enough men to work on the track.
I believe that railway accidents ought to be investigated by the railways and by the CTC. Quite definitely, a public statement ought to be made on such accidents. Many dangerous situations, if brought to the public's attention, could be eliminated. I certainly agree with and support the hon. member for Moncton.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate in the debate on Bill C-ll, an Act to Amend the Railway Act, which has been brought in by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) considering that for these past few years the issue of security on our railways has become more important than ever, especially in the Province of Quebec with the many derailments that occurred in the months of November and December, 1972, and January, 1973.
The bill now before us proposes the appointment of one or many persons competent to inquire into the causes and circumstances of railway accidents in order to prevent other accidents. The bill also calls for a report to be made public in such cases.
Mr. Speaker, we should examine this bill carefully and also we should dismiss the idea that it has been introduced by a back-bencher. The proposal is very interest-
January 30, 1973

ing, as the hon. member for Saint-Boniface (Mr. Guay) said, and the government should take it into consideration. No activity is free of danger and we shall never manage to prevent all accidents. Still, we can reduce their seriousness to a minimum in every field.
Mr. Speaker, I have visited Canada from east to west in the trains of our two railway companies and, despite some of their problems, I admit that they serve the people adequately and that the railroaders are familiar with then-routes. The railwaymen who are manning trains in the Rockies are to be congratulated since they work in very dangerous places. However, very few accidents are reported in the canyons of the Rockies where landslides are rather frequent.
A few years ago, we still had steam engines which could haul 50-odd cars. However, through the years, we have succeeded in building diesel engines which are more powerful and which nowadays can pull up to 150 cars.
It remains to be seen whether the technology of security has progressed at the same rate as the design of these powerful machines. As some of my colleagues will point out the railway companies have perhaps not brought comparable improvements to the security of railroads and passengers.
When we talk with diesel engineers who have to take those huge trains throughout the country, they agree with us that there are some dangers. They tell us that it is almost impossible to stop a train when they see an obstacle on the tracks.
The Canadian Transport Commission conducts regular studies in this field and an inquiry is now under way on security conditions of our railways. I congratulate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) as well as the Chairman of the Transport Commission on their prompt inquiries into the causes of major accidents which occurred on our railways during the past few years.
Mr. Speaker, it should now be pointed out in this House that 10 years ago there were some forty crossings on the railroad between Matapedia and Gaspe, all of which, thanks to the co-operation of the Canadian Transport Commission and the government of the province of Quebec, are to be eliminated from Highway 6 which girdles the Gaspe Peninsula within the next three years.
Such improvements to the highway network will certainly facilitate traffic and the people of the Gaspe peninsula and their visitors will greatly enjoy driving along a highway free of railway crossings.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I shall say that there is always room for improvement in the field of railway security and I urge the House to adopt Bill 11 now before us.

Be it as it may, the subject matter of his bill interests me considerably, not to say that it fascinates me in a way,

because since my election here in 1968 I have done the utmost to clarify all sorts of answers from the heads of various Canadian railway companies concerning accidents, number of passengers who use their lines and so on.
I even felt discouraged on occasion because every time I asked a question, they found all sorts of reasons for not answering. Mr. Speaker, I think we expected a little more from the parliamentary secretary than that. This is a matter of economics, and inasmuch as we have been here for a month and have not passed a piece of legislation that affects the economy I think before we get into committee of the whole there are one or two observations which should be made.
First of all, I hope that the government is aware of the serious situation that will exist at the port of Halifax and St. John's, as well as the river ports, in view of the tremendous increases that are going to come about as a result of the provisions of this bill. In some cases it will mean an immediate 60 per cent increase and in other cases the increase will be 180 per cent or 200 per cent. No one in Canada objects to paying for what are essentially good services and there is no question that these services are needed for the conduct of vessels in and out of the ports and restricted sailing areas. No one objects to paying just fees; what is objected to is the situation where receivers of pilotage services in Canada are being forced to pay through the nose. That is a matter of regret.
Another matter of regret, Mr. Speaker, which I think must be expressed before we move on is the fact that the government has had 19 months in which to make consequential or substantive amendments to the clauses of the bill that needed change. They apparently miscalculated to the tune of a couple of billion dollars in an area in which judgment played a role. I wonder how on earth they could have misjudged the length of time it was going to take Mr. Mahoney to complete his study of the Canada Shipping Act, if this is in fact the reason why this House is tonight faced with a deadline.
Surely something more could be expected from the parliamentary secretary than his cursory remarks. This type of housekeeping legislation, if it is so urgent, should have been the very first thing placed before us a month ago; instead of that we have it tonight because the deadline is February 1 [DOT]
I do not think there is any point in getting into some of the details of the bill at this stage. Perhaps on second reading or during the committee stage the parliamentary secretary will explain why. after seven months in one sense and 19 months in the other sense, the government now wants an additional year. Perhaps he could tell us a little about the way Mr. Mahoney's work stands, and when we might expect to have a revision of the Canada Shipping Act before us so that we can do something about the pilotage legislation on a more permanent basis.
Perhaps over the next minute or two he would consider giving the committee some indication of what the government intends with respect to their reaction to the appeals that are being filed. I know that in a sense this is a little out of the context of our discussion in this House because it may become a matter for the courts, but perhaps the parliamentary secretary would give some indication of the government's position.

Mr. Speaker, as was indicated earlier, there is a disposition to expedite the passage of this bill. However, I am sure other members must wonder, as I do, why on the eve of the expiration of the extension of the old bylaws and regulations the government comes along and asks for another extension for one year. The short answer, of course, is that the new bills and new regulations in respect of the various pilotage authorities and areas are not yet ready.
However, what really disturbs me, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that by tomorrow midnight, in my interpretation of what this bill means and what the Pilotage Act means, there will be a void, a vacuum, a situation in which there are no rules and regulations and no bylaws regarding the operation of ships in Canada unless this particular piece of legislation is passed. The extension that was available in the current law expires tomorrow at midnight. I can conceive of a pretty chaotic situation in the various areas and districts of Canada that are affected by the Pilotage Act. The old rules and regulations will disappear and there will not be any new ones to take their place.
According to people I have spoken to on the west coast there is tremendous concern about the period when a vacuum will exist. One thing that could happen is this. The new draft bylaws, rules and regulations which were to be the subject of consultation with the shipping and towboat industry may, if this bill is not passed, be put into effect out of desperation by the pilotage authorities because nothing else will be available to them: their old rules will be gone; they will have only the draft rules. Out of desperation, in order to have some kind of regulation or bylaw in force on February 1 they may put into effect a half-baked set of rules that will cause chaos. If that situation prevails, this government will be entirely to blame for waiting until the last possible moment to ask for an additional one-year extension.
We have given unanimous consent to bailing out the government. This indicates the concern of members of the House about this matter. Also, we respect the rights of the shipping industry. However, in the process of the bill going through the legislative machinery there could be a vacuum between here, the Senate and royal assent. I hope there will not. It is regrettable that the government, through the parliamentary secretary, should wait until the last possible moment, when we are on the brink of a confused and chaotic situation, to ask us to help them out of this desperate position. Naturally, we are concerned about this because of the situation that could exist with regard to shipping in Canada. We want to do everything we can to assist.
I have not seen the draft bylaws or regulations that are proposed for the west coast. I do not know if they apply to other parts of Canada as well. I have been informed that the draft form is so rigid that it imposes a straitjacket type of regulation on the towboat industry. This is a local type of towing. These boats tow from port to port in British Columbia. The skippers of these towboats know the waters in their areas far better than any pilot because theirs is a year-round operation. I hope these draft bylaws are not put into effect; if they are, a towboat skipper will have to take a pilot aboard to move from one side of
Pilotage Act
Vancouver harbour to the other. That is stupid and ridiculous. This industry knows more about shipping and moving barges and logs on the coast of British Columbia than any pilot or the Department of Transport, yet that is the situation that prevails.
In this extension of one year, I hope that whoever is responsible for drafting the bylaws that apply to the west coast, and possibly to other parts of Canada, will have enough common sense to make them meaningful and workable in the industry. I hope that those who are wrapped up in the bureaucratic concept of their own importance and cannot see beyond the paper they are writing on, cannot see beyond their office and cannot look into the industry to see what is happening, will be removed from those positions so that common sense can prevail in the drafting of the bylaws and regulations. I hope the minister, his parliamentary secretary or whoever is piloting this bill through the House will respond to the concerns I have expressed on behalf of those who will be affected by the current draft proposals.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to give hon. members some additional information. The Pilotage Act, Section 43(4), provided that "every bylaw made or expressed to have been made by a pilotage authority as defined in the Canada Shipping Act and every regulation made pursuant to part VII of that act and in force, or deemed to be in force, on the commencement of this Act, continues in force unless the bylaw or regulation is revoked by an authority." The bylaws and regulations referred to in this subsection covered the operations of each pilotage district, including such matters as the licensing of pilots, examinations, collection of dues, dispatching of pilots, entry into the pilotage service, assignment to duty, discipline and other matters respecting the regulating of pilot service and tariff schedules for each of the 29 districts which were operated under the Canada Shipping Act.
Since their establishment the authorities have been required to negotiate with pilots of the various districts within their regions. Under the act, pilots may elect to be employees of the authority or to contract their services through their association. The authorities could not establish new pilotage tariffs until negotiations with the pilots were completed, and they have found it impossible to

adopt new bylaws and regulations prior to the expiration of the old bylaws and regulations because of unavoidable delays involved in rendering operable their administrative structures and in negotiating new tariffs with representatives of the pilots and industry to provide for their operating costs and allow for increases in wages demanded by the pilots.
Furthermore, some of the tariffs proposed were objected to under section 23 of the Pilotage Act. When an objection is filed before the Canadian Transport Commission a tariff is held in abeyance until such time as the objection is disposed of by the CTC. It may be some time before hearings are held by the commission and a decision is reached on the contentious items of the tariffs.
Due to the reasons I have outlined, no new regulations or bylaws were enacted establishing compulsory pilotage areas or prescribing ships or classes of ships to which compulsory pilotage applies. It is believed that the proposed regulations or bylaws on compulsory pilotage areas and ships will also be objected to by representatives of the pilots or the industry under section 14(3) of the act, entailing further delays before regulations on this subject are implemented.

True, all this is supposition. It may be that the Senate, contrary to its usual practice, moves with speed and dispatch and deals with this bill tomorrow. However, I am convinced that the government is not resting its whole case on the hope that parliament will give speedy passage to the bill. Although it received unanimous consent to deal with the bill this evening, the Senate may not give its unanimous consent and consider the bill in one day, with the Governor General then hustling down here tomorrow night to give royal assent to the bill. I think we are entitled to know what are the government's contingency plans, and so is the shipping industry.
I have another question I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary. As I understand it, unless the schedule has been altered there is in existence the Atlantic Pilotage Authority, a distinct authority with its office in Halifax. Its region is the Atlantic seaboard, the Atlantic coast. There is also in existence another pilotage authority known as the Laurentian Pilotage Authority. Its head office is in Montreal and its region of activity is the northern entrance to St. Lambert's lock and that general area. There is also the Great Lakes Pilotage Authority with headquarters in Cornwall, its region being all the waters in the province of Quebec south of the northern entrance to St. Lambert lock and all Canadian waters in and around the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba-in other words, the Great Lakes. There is also the Pacific Pilotage Authority which governs the waters along the Pacific coast.
I should like to know whether negotiations have been taking place with each of these pilotage authorities but have been stalled. Has each of these pilotage authorities been unable to reach a conclusive agreement with the pilots? I think we also require to know what is the position of the draft bylaws of each of these pilotage authorities. Are they incomplete, are they just proposals, are they waiting for some response from the industry in regard to whether or not they are acceptable, and does each of them require this additional one year's extension?
Another question I think we are entitled to have answered is this. I very much regret I have not yet had an opportunity to determine what authority is given by part VII of the Canada Shipping Act to make regulations. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when preparing my few remarks for this evening I was reminded of the situation where, if you take your research material from one source, in effect you are copying, but if you take it from several sources, that comes under the glorified heading of research. Each member who has participated in this debate has done a tremendous amount of research and a great deal of soul-searching. The speeches I have heard so far give clear evidence that a great deal of reading has been done by hon. members, which has served to elevate the calibre of the debate.
I want to put my position on the record and the reasons for the stand that I am taking. I believe that the death penalty is an immature response to an irrational act. I believe that advocates of capital punishment for murder are looking for an easy solution. There is not one. I am indebted to the Rev. George Goth who had an article in the London Free Press on this subject, on January 13 of this year. I would like to quote a few extracts from it:
To be sure, I do not accept the voice of experts and statistics as final. None the less, it does need to be said that criminologists, by and large, do not believe that capital punishment acts as a deterrent. Violence creates violence.
If I may digress for a moment here, I would refer to the splendid address given by the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner) when he dealt with the question of deterrence. Returning to the Rev. Goth's article:
To the argument that homicide is on the increase since the death penalty has been stopped the answer is very simple. Most crimes have increased dramatically in the past ten years. The reason for this is not a more cavalier treatment of the criminal. Let us rid ourselves of North American conceit. We belong to a violent society. Respect for authority has gone with the wind . . .
We are living in a post-Christian era. The old order has died. No new one has come to take its place.
Faced with this, we in this House have a particular responsibility and certainly the government's responsibility increases day by day. The Rev. Goth makes the following points against the imposition of capital punishment, which he says does not meet the real problem. He writes:
January 30, 1973

There is no evidence that it will serve as a deterrent.
It would be a cheap evasion of the real causes of crime.
It is unworthy of any civilized state. Vengeance is not a mature response to an irrational act.
Violence creates violence. The state must not reduce itself to the level of the criminal.
We are looking for a simple answer and there is none. The way ahead will be long and hard.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to the comments made by the hon. member for Thunder Bay I should like to refer hon. members to the statements made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) and his timely comments yesterday. I have listened very carefully to the debate, and those speeches that I missed I have read. I must say that the calibre of the addresses has been high. This is due in no small measure to the fact that it is a free vote despite the occasion taken by some to launch cheap political shots. I think the tone and calibre of the debate is high also because there are good arguments to be made on both sides of the issue.
I was somewhat surprised, however, to hear my friend, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), suggest yesterday that there is little room for error in our present courts system. I suggest to him that the courts system is a long way from being infallible and I think there are better arguments he could use than those that the courts nowadays are not very likely to make an error.
We have used the M'Naghten rule in dealing with the criminally insane for all too long a period, and although today psychiatrists can be called as expert witnesses it is extremely difficult on many occasions to convince a jury of schizophrenia, paranoia or other problems of the mind that would lead an individual to kill. But aside from all of that, I think we must be aware of the fact there is daily a possibility of error creeping into judicial decisions. Crowded court calendars increase this ever-present danger. There is always the danger of executing an innocent person. Mr. Dahn Batchelor writes in the current issue of the "International Review," and I agree:
One of the greatest arguments against capital punishment is the danger of executing an innocent person. No miscarriage of justice is more terrible to contemplate. The execution of the innocent generally results from three types of testimony: the first is circumstantial. It is impossible to dispense with circumstantial evidence. If such evidence was not permitted to be heard in a court of law, criminals could laugh at the laws because a legally sane person rarely commits murder in front of witnesses.
Mr. Speaker, the courts recognize that it is often necessary to rely on circumstantial evidence, but they also know it is dangerous to do so. I should like, as many of my colleagues have done, to relate a personal experience that perhaps more than anything else convinced me that mistakes could be made and that we should be extremely careful. I will alter the circumstances a little to protect my client and the other parties involved, but the circumstances are true.
Some years ago, an elderly couple in their seventies were viciously beaten by, they said, three men. The licence number of the car used by the criminals had been secured and the police, through a splendid bit of investigatory work, eventually charged three men. One of the three men came into my office and indicated that they
Capital Punishment
had in fact been together all day long, and this was established. He also indicated to me that they had done a tremendous amount of drinking. It is significant that this man did not know whether he had in fact participated in the beating up and the robbery, but he thought the likelihood was very good that he had although he assured me he had absolutely no memory of the incident; and in light of the amount of alcohol that had been consumed by him that day, I believed him.
Relying, however, on the necessity of the Crown to establish its case, a plea of not guilty was entered on behalf of this particular individual. In a subsequent interview with him I asked if time had helped his memory, had given him any reason to believe that he had participated or that he had not. He indicated that he established with his landlord the exact time that he had come into the house. Because he was actually at that particular time some 20 miles away from the scene of the crime, he began to wonder if he had, in fact, participated in the savage beating and robbery.
When we retraced his steps it was determined that he had left the company of the other individuals. The three men had driven off in the car, but subsequently he got out of the vehicle and went to a restaurant. We were able to find someone there who remembered him, not only because he had been violently ill in the restaurant but also because he had neglected to pay his bill. It was established that he had been in the restaurant at the time the vicious and brutal beating had taken place. I wondered at the time, Mr. Speaker, if we had not been able to locate that witness in the restaurant and if the elderly couple, or one of them had been killed, whether this man, not knowing whether he had participated, could have been hanged for this particular offence.
Aside from errors in the courts, Mr. Speaker, there are errors that creep in as a result of circumstances in particular cases. This case convinced me in dramatic fashion that it is possible to make a mistake. As I say, I wondered whether this man would have been found guilty of murder if one of the couple had died, or whether he would have served a long prison sentence if we had been unable to establish his innocence. He could not, in effect, go into the witness-box and proclaim his innocence because he did not know whether he had participated.
Mr. Speaker, it was exciting this afternoon to hear the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) answer the question that I think is on the minds of many of us. Many of us have answered it to our satisfaction. I do not feel that I came down here as someone to pass on what I think the majority of people in my riding would do in the circumstances, to act as a computer card punch-out. I think I have an obligation to use such intelligence as I have to vote as I see fit.
The retentionist is in the enviable position of not having to pull the cord that opens the trapdoor, to pull the switch nor, for that matter, to drop the gas vial into the gas chamber. I think in the heat of the moment almost anyone could kill in the interest of protecting a member of his or her family, or in the interest of protecting a fellow human being from a vicious attack. This is done without thinking in the heat of the moment, and I think it is possible for most people. However, I wonder if a year later, after the

January 30, 1973
Capital Punishment
passion had been dispelled, after the heat of the moment and after the victim had long been buried, whether one person could go into a cell and hand another a cyanide tablet and say, "This is retribution for the heinous crime you committed " I think it is unlikely. The right hon. gentleman this afternoon pointed out very clearly that these hangings, these killings do not take place in public. If we are going to use that as a deterrent, surely in public is where society should say it should take place.
Mr. Speaker, I take strong exception to those who say that we abolitionists are backed into a corner; in other words, that we have more concern for the accused than we have for the victim. Of course this is not the case; this just cannot be true. I have no sympathy-my heart is filled with revulsion at the thought that one individual would take the life of another.
When the Solicitor General (Mr. AUmand) in his remarks mentioned that the first hanging in Canada was that of a 16-year-old girl, I think that filled most of us with revulsion. Had that taken place last night I do not think that one person in this House would have agreed with it. We have come a long way in 150 years, Mr. Speaker, and I think the time has come for abolition. I am going to support this bill, but I hope amendments will be introduced at the committee stage. I am not at present a member of the committee; that is why I want to make one or two remarks about my attitude.
Because I am an abolitionist, I think more than ever we have an obligation to society to protect society and so I abhor the situation where an individual who takes a life, a sexual offender, a psychopathic killer, is granted leave of absence or parole after a ten-year period. I think something must be done to protect society and that is why I feel, as an abolitionist, that individuals who kill other individuals should be put in prison; whether it be for a period of 20 or 25 years could be argued, it is academic, but the time has come to stop these ridiculous, easy paroles.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in any debate, when it comes time for the thirtieth or thirty-fifth speaker, or whatever I am, to stand and say a few words, that person wonders what he can possibly contribute to the debate. I expect the answer is always, very little. What I am really doing this evening is giving a personal testimony rather than attempting to influence the outcome of the debate, since most of the arguments on either side of this case have been presented very ably by members who
(Mr. Cullen.)
preceded me. There are a few things which are peripheral to the issue but they may have a bearing on the thinking of some members of this House. I want to draw these to the attention of the House before dealing with the main issues.
Some participants in this debate, notably the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), seem to consider it. to be a sort of interlude between discussions of more difficult and socially important legislation. There is a certain element of hypocrisy in the legislation before us, legislation which continues the practice of restricting capital punishment to murderers of policemen and prison guards. Most of us cannot conceive of a Canadian cabinet reversing the practice of more than a decade and failing to exercise the royal prerogative of mercy on behalf of someone convicted of murder.
As appropriate as the remarks of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) were this afternoon when he said, in effect, "The law is the law; the cabinet must obey it. If it does not like it, it must change it," it is extremely unlikely that a cabinet would change the practice of the past decade or more. Like the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), I would be much happier if we were completely honest with ourselves and the country and dealt with arguments for and against the abolition of capital punishment on their merits, avoiding the kind of obfuscation incorporated in the bill before us.
Having said that, I cannot associate myself with those who argue that the question of whether or not to retain the death penalty should be of relatively low legislative priority. To me, the outcome of this debate will reveal the general level of civilization, sophistication, compassion and understanding in Canadian society. It will also help to determine the level of civilization, sophistication, compassion and understanding in the years to come, because laws do change social attitudes. For that reason, this debate is important.
The debate is also important because the people of this country are telling us it is important. I very much doubt that any member at this moment is receiving more mail on any other subject. Public interest is revealed also in the response to questionnaires sent out by members. Returns of questionnaires which avoided the question of capital punishment have been much lower than returns of questionnaires which asked for opinions on the issue.
I entered this debate only after a considerable amount of soul-searching both with respect to the merits of the case and having decided that total abolition of the death penalty represents the greatest public good with respect to the correctness of taking a stand which would not seem to be in accord with that taken by a majority of my constituents, at least a majoi'ity of those who have taken the trouble to acquaint me with their views.
I feel obliged to inform the House, even in speaking for abolition of the death penalty, that returns of my questionnaire, about 3,000 of them now out of 35,000 mailed, confirm the results of similar unscientific, and I emphasize that word, surveys, conducted over the past few months by newspapers, magazines and the electronics media. In the returns of my questionnaire there is overwhelming support for the retention of the dealth penalty.
January 30, 1973

In retrospect, I believe that a more careful wording of the questionnaire would have modified the results of the questionnaire somewhat but would have left a majority of opinion in favour of retention of the death penalty.
Some grade 11 students from Lord Selkirk regional comprehensive secondary school in my constituency conducted a much more careful survey of 1,000 people on the issue of capital punishment. They discovered that in excess of 50 per cent of those polled favoured retention of the death penalty and only 36 per cent of the adults wanted abolition. I have lived in my constituency since I was 11 years old. I feel very much a part of it. I am saddened by the seeming fact that a majority of my neighbours do not believe, as I do, that capital punishment must be abolished. Yet I will vote for abolition in this House, or as near as I can come to abolition of the death penalty. What gives me that right? How can I, as an elected representative, vote against what would seem to be the wishes of the majority of my constituents at this moment?
Other members in attempting to explain their taking similar action, that is voting for abolition, referred to or quoted John Stuart Mill and Edmund Burke on the difference between a delegate and a representative. Stripped of their elitist language, both Burke's statement to the electors of Bristol and Locke's passage in an essay on representative government help to explain my position. Put simply, I believe that as an elected representative I have been sent here to exercise my judgment based upon the best information available to me, and that one of the most important pieces of information upon which I base any judgment is my assessment of the opinion of my electorate at any given moment. The opinion of my electorate always remains one of my most important considerations. It is always taken into account. However, there must be other considerations as well. In the final count, the opinion of my electorate must remain just one consideration, however important that one consideration may be.
I am not a delegate. Our system, I believe wisely, does not require me to poll my constituents on every issue and vote according to the results of that poll. If after reflection my constituents believe my judgment to have been faulty, their remedy lies in the polling booth. It is my hope that they will never feel obliged to resort to that remedy, but in the final analysis I must live with myself and my conscience.
Capital punishment is an emotionally charged issue. It is the duty of a politician, when dealing with such an issue, to attempt to divorce himself from emotion and to make his decision on the basis of logic and the facts before him. If that means occasionally acting contrary to the immediate wishes of his constituents-and such occasions will present themselves only rarely-then so acting is his duty. There are few Canadians today who do not wish that more of their politicians had possessed the courage or the judgment to oppose the internment of Canadian-Japanese and the confiscation of their property during World War II, although public opinion at the time was overwhelmingly in favour of the action taken by the government. I wonder, in that regard, how public opinion would be expressing itself in relation to capital punishment today if yesterday we had discovered that the state
Capital Punishment
had hanged an innocent man or woman, something which has happened in the past.
The advocates of the retention of capital punishment have never yet answered Lafayette's challenge, "I shall ask for the abolition of the penalty of death until the infallibility of human judgment has been demonstrated to me." The hon. member for Calgary North tried to answer this challenge yesterday but I believe he failed to do so. No one can say how many innocent persons have been murdered by the courts. Consider the opportunities for error, the opportunity for false testimony to be given, the possibility of mistaken identification, the possibility of a biased jury, the possibility of evidence being misinterpreted. I could go on.
Responsible estimates of the proportion of innocent persons among those executed run as high as 5 per cent. But even if the figure is only .5 per cent, the argument against capital punishment because of the possibility of judicial error is a powerful one. That a judicial error may occur, even if only rarely, is sufficient reason to avoid exacting the penalty of death. I believe society should never lay claim to absolute authority over life.
Why do so many Canadians at this point in time wish to retain the death penalty? Part of the reason lies in the fact that we are disturbed, even frightened by the pace of change, social and technological, in our society. We seem to be losing control over important events which affect our daily lives. We set up a complicated system to ensure a reasonable standard of life for those people who have suffered misfortune-people who for illness or some other reason are no longer capable of providing for themselves-and we see people for whom the system was never intended benefiting from it. We pay our taxes and for the most part we obey the laws which govern us; we avoid temptations to cheat and steal and to take advantage of our neighbours. Yet we see others almost literally getting away with murder.
We search desperately for a touchstone, some evidence of permanence and certitude in a world increasingly characterized by change. And our search is without success. This leads to frustration, to a desire to lash out and assert ourselves As a result, some citizens commit crimes of violence. The rest of us react by saying, "Kill them", thinking perhaps that in so doing a danger to our lives and to the lives around us may be removed and that others so inclined might be frightened away from such action.
To such thinking I pose two principal objections. The first is that we as a society have no right to take the life of any person. The second is that state-sanctioned murder probably accomplishes no real purpose in any event. The first argument is a moral one. I appreciate that there are sincere, concerned people who will disagree with me on moral grounds. For many of us, this is a matter of interpretation. What do we do when in one place a guide book to moral behaviour says, "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed" and in another place seriously questions the moral authority of judge and executioner, "Let him that is without sin cast the first stone"?
806

January 30, 1973
Capital Punishment
I hope that this debate will not see numbers of members quoting the Bible as an authority for the retention of the death penalty. If such does happen, there are other members of my party who are better equipped than me to offer rebuttal. But in anticipation I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to a passage from a publication put out by the Institute of Mennonite Studies:
A close study of these earliest chapters of the Bible shows that the death penalty as stated there is clearly not so much a requirement as a limitation. It is spoken against the background of a story of corruption in which vengeance was the general pattern . ..
Let us, therefore, begin realistically as the Bible does. Vengeance does not need to be commanded; it happens. It is the normal response of fallen man to any situation which calls for his hostility. And normally such vengeance is unlimited.
Most primitive peoples show the same pattern of vengeance as the Old Testament peoples for whom the rules in the Bible were initially established. In such societies it is normal for vengeance and counter-vengeance to raise the toll of suffering brought about by any offence far beyond proportion to the original damage done. Limits have been set, as in the Old Testament. But I believe it to be a terrible distortion to interpret this practical solution, to limit punishment to the actual wrongdoer, as providing some sort of sanction for the death penalty. On the contrary, I believe the most powerful assertion of my heritage is in favour of the sanctity of human life.
I want no part in a decision, even a collective decision, which leads to the taking of sentient human life. Murder of any sort, in any circumstances, even in the course of an execution, is never moral and it should not be legal. In "Spirits Rebellious," the Lebanese philosopher, Kahlil Gibran, comes across the corpses of three people who have been executed for committing crimes. He writes:
Three human beings who yesterday were in the lap of life today fell as victims to death because they broke the rules of human society. When a man kills another man, the people say he is murderer, but when the Emir kills him, the Emir is just. When a man robs a monastery, they say he is a thief but when the Emir robs such a man of his life, the Emir is honourable.
Shedding of blood is forbidden. But who made it lawful for the Emir? Stealing money is a crime, but taking away one's life is a noble act. Shall we meet evil with evil and say this is the law? Shall we fight corruption with greater corruption and say this is the rule? Shall we conquer crimes with more crimes, and say this is justice?
I said earlier that some people are leaning toward retention because they feel capital punishment may reduce the number of murders committed. This theory of deterrence is undoubtedly the most serious of the social arguments for the retention of the death penalty. It is argued that if persons who are tempted to commit a crime know in advance what the punishment will be, they will turn away from committing such a crime. Superficially this appears to be a sensible argument. It is the argument put forward by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) on Friday.
However, that the argument is basically in error can be seen clearly upon closer examination. A major source of the error is the assumption that murder is like speeding and that a normal person, through fear of being caught, will refrain from it out of consideration for the consequences. But the fallacy is this: murderers are not normal people, for the most part. Most of them are driven by forces of emotion, or outright insanity even, to such an

extent that no reasoning takes place at all; there is no weighing of consequences as they proceed to kill. I am not necessarily making a plea that such people ought to be pitied; it is a demand that we understand the circumstances in which they are, for the most part, incapable of reacting and reasoning like normal human beings.
Thus to attempt, as did the hon. member for Crowfoot, to draw a parallel between the noose and the breathalyzer is at best foolish. Numerous psychological studies have made this fact clear. In committing murder, people for the most part are committing an insane act and are not capable of reasoning rationally. I think the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) this afternoon cited studies made of skyjackers, but there are other cases on record where unbalanced persons lacking the strength of will to kill themselves have committed murder or other violent acts as an indirect act of suicide. Here the death penalty is an encouragement to murder, not a deterrent. A small minority of murderers are professional criminals for whom death is simply one of the occupational hazards. They are also reasonably sure of avoiding capture, or if captured of avoiding conviction, or if convicted of avoiding execution.
The error of the deterrent theory can also be shown statistically. I do not intend to cite the great tables of statistics that are available, because this would take up too much time. In addition, such statistics are vulnerable to subjective interpretation and most of the statistics available have already been cited by other participants in this debate. However, I will cite the judgments of objective studies which have analysed the statistics. These studies have consistently found that there is absolutely no valid evidence to prove that the death penalty has any deterrent value whatever. This has been the finding generally throughout the western world and it has led country after country to abolish capital punishment over the course of the past 100 years. There are now probably in excess of 70 jurisdictions in the world that have abolished capital punishment.
In 1953 the British royal commission on capital punishment concluded that there is no clear evidence that homicide rates are influenced by the death penalty or by the frequency of executions. The New Jersey commission to study capital punishment found that the death penalty could not be demonstrated to be a more effective deterrent than life imprisonment. In Canada the joint committee on capital punishment reported on June 27, 1957, that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent, that it had no unique deterrent effect that could not be accomplished by imprisonment.
Ten years ago the United Nations published a report questioning the deterrent value of the death penalty in which it said that data showed no correlation between the existence of the death penalty and the incidence of murder. More recently, Dr. Fattah of the University of Montreal once again demonstrated in an objective study that a case cannot be made for the deterrent value of capital punishment.
I shall not waste time exchanging interpretations of statistics with hon. members who wish to retain the death
January 30, 1973

penalty, but I will say this. If there is dispute about the meaning of the statistics-and I would admit the possibility-then the burden of proof rests on those who wish the state to commit murder. There is a powerful moral argument against killing a person even by way of judicial execution. To support their position, those in favour of the retention of capital punishment, by any standard of justice, must present evidence beyond reasonable doubt that executions have some beneficial social effect. So far in this debate I submit they have not done so.
I am convinced that the people of Canada do not lust after the blood of murderers. I am convinced that if at the moment the majority tend to favour capital punishment, it is because they want an assurance that their lives and the lives of their loved ones will not be placed in jeopardy because of inadequacies in our penal system, our parole system and the totally and completely inadequate attempts at rehabilitation in penal institutions.
I am convinced that if the people of Canada could see avenues to explore other than the death penalty in the search for security from crimes of violence, they would eagerly explore them. To the extent that we as elected politicians have not made .it apparent to Canadians that other avenues do exist, we have failed the Canadian people. We should be looking, for example, at indeterminate sentences for crimes of violence. We should be looking, until we can bolster and render effective our efforts at rehabilitation and at making our parole system effective, at longer mandatory sentences for those who commit violent crimes. We should be seeking effective psychiatric services for those in our penal institutions. Finally and most importantly, we should be seeking the means to remove the social causes, the inequalities, the injustices, the uncertainties, the frustrations that foster and nourish crimes of violence.
However this debate is decided-and I fervently hope it is decided in a manner that will bring us closer to the total elimination of the death penalty-we will be failing ourselves and our electorate if we do not immediately begin work on providing real measures of security for Canadians; and I submit that the death penalty does not provide any real measure of security. We shall have failed if we do not immediately begin work on improving our penal system; to ensure that our penal system is capable of rehabilitating criminals; to ensure that until that rehabilitation is complete, possibilities for parole do not exist; to ensure that until our penal system is capable of accomplishing rehabilitation we do not admit persons to the streets who are incapable of undertaking their responsibilities as citizens.
This is the kind of action we must take. We must immediately begin the task of removing the injustices, frustrations and uncertainties that produce crimes of violence. Once this debate is finished this must be our task; otherwise this debate will have been pointless and we will have failed in our duties as legislators.

the land. Had the government been attuned to the public pulse it would have heard the refrain, "Bring back capital punishment.
